Background and Aims: Aphasia is a communication disorder that occurs in approximately 30% of all stroke survivors. Because of their communication issues, few studies have examined how people with aphasia (PWA) perceive the accessibility, satisfaction, and affordability of post-stroke healthcare services.
Methods: Using the 2019-2022 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), panel data regression compared the perceived accessibility, satisfaction with healthcare and affordability of healthcare of 404 PWA to 4,120 stroke survivors without aphasia.
Results: When compared to stroke survivors without aphasia, PWA who were female and those earning low incomes were more likely to spend more than 15 minutes traveling to their usual source of care (USC). Black and Hispanic PWA were also more likely than White PWA to feel that their provider did not explain all treatment options or ask them to help decide on their treatment. Finally, Black PWA were more likely to have difficulty paying their medical bills than White PWA.
Conclusions: PWA and particularly those from racial-ethnic minority and low-income backgrounds experienced greater difficulty accessing healthcare and are more likely to be less satisfied with their healthcare than their counterparts. Similarly, they experienced greater difficulty financing their healthcare.

Background and Aims: Peru experiences a high incidence of ischemic stroke, leading to a higher rate of morbimortality, yet comprehensive data on stroke care infrastructure and practices remain scarce. This study aimed to assess the perceptions and experiences of healthcare personal, identifying gaps in care organization, resource availability, and awareness of stroke centers.
Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 83 healthcare professionals from diverse Peruvian healthcare institutions, using an structured electronic survey.
Results: 49.4% were neurologists, 26.5% emergency physicians, and 24.1% nurses. Most (94.9%) had received stroke care training. Non-contrast cranial CT was available in 97.6% of centers, with 97.5% offering 24/7 access. However, only 32.5% had access to CT angiography, and 34.9% to MRI. Regarding stroke detection, 59.8% used FAST, while 10.9% employed NIHSS. Continuous stroke care was reported by 91.6% of respondents, and 84.3% indicated the presence of a stroke care protocol in their centers. Pre-notification systems were lacking in 43.9% of facilities. Although 97.6% had access to fibrinolytics, 72.4% did not utilize them, citing reasons such as imaging delays and fear of complications. Mechanical thrombectomy was unavailable in 59.8% of centers. The primary barrier to effective stroke treatment identified was the population’s lack of symptom recognition (60.7%)
Conclusions: The survey revealed significant disparities in stroke care across Peru, including inconsistent access to advanced imaging, underutilization of thrombolytic therapy, and limited availability of mechanical thrombectomy. These findings highlight the need for national policies to standardize stroke care, enhance public awareness, and improve resource allocation to optimize outcomes for patients with stroke in Peru.

HEALTH SERVICES.W.J. Liu1, R. Wang1, L. Lemke1, G. Bonifacio1, J. Kamara2, R. Kestur1, R. Marigold1
1University Hospital Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom, 2Queen Alexandra Hospital, Portsmouth, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Rising stroke service demand in the UK is partly driven by patients with mild symptoms. The National Optimal Stroke Imaging pathway recommends an MRI within 1 hour in cases of mild symptoms and/or diagnostic uncertainty. Prompt imaging facilitates treatment and patient flow. The stroke same day emergency care (SDEC) offers rapid same day investigations and treatment for patients presenting with mild symptoms and low probability of stroke. This study aims to investigate MRI wait times in patients presenting with mild stroke symptoms (NIHSS⩽4) and assess whether a stroke SDEC pathway reduces MRI wait time.
Methods: A retrospective study was conducted in the stroke department at a single tertiary centre. Data were collected from the advanced care practitioner stroke referral database during two 6-week periods: pre-SDEC (23/09/24–03/11/24) and during the SDEC pilot (04/11/24–16/12/24). Patients with NIHSS⩽4 were included; patients with no adequate documentation or seen in TIA/outpatient clinics were excluded.
Results: During the pre-SDEC period, 73 patients had NIHSS⩽4 and 52 had MRIs with a mean wait time of 16h33m; 86% were admitted to a stroke ward. During the SDEC pilot, 104 patients had NIHSS⩽4; average MRI wait time was 11h34m and 66% were admitted to the stroke unit. Of the 40 patients with NIHSS⩽4 seen in SDEC, 29 had MRIs with an average wait time of 3h50m. MRI wait times were significantly lower during the SDEC trial period (p=0.016).
Conclusions: The stroke SDEC pathway significantly reduced MRI wait times in patients presenting with mild symptoms and admissions to the stroke unit.

HEALTH SERVICES.R. Li, J. Li, Y. Jin, B. Lin

Background and Aims: Stroke is considered one of the leading causes of both death and disability in the world. Facial expression recognition (FER), a technology within the realm of computer vision, enables the timely and accurate detection of changes in facial expressions. It has found broad application in the medical field. However, the existing evidence regarding the application and value of FER in stroke is limited.
Methods: Studies on applications of facial expression recognition in stroke were retrieved in PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI and WanFang databases from inception to September 2024.

Future research should focus on developing and validating algorithms or models with excellent performance, and expanding the application of FER in the field of stroke.

DESIGN PRINCIPLES FOR A STANDARDIZED CLINICAL ASSESSMENT TOOL TO IMPROVE MODIFIED RANKIN SCALE CONSISTENCY
HEALTH SERVICES.L. London1, N. Kamal2
1Dalhousie University, Industrial Engineering, Halifax, Canada, 2Dalhousie University, Department Of Industrial Engineering, Halifax, Canada
Background and Aims: The Modified Rankin Scale (mRS) is a widely used tool for assessing disability in stroke care; however, its administration is often affected by subjectivity and variability, leading to poor inter-rater reliability and inconsistencies in scoring. Originally developed for hospital discharge evaluations, the mRS evolved into a tool for long-term disability assessment and clinical decision-making. Inconsistencies persist due to a lack of standardization, subjective judgment, and cognitive biases during its administration. This paper aims to develop design principles for a standardized Clinical Assessment Tool (CAT) to support more reliable and usable mRS administration across care settings.
Methods: The design principles of the CAT are grounded in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and cognitive engineering. The proposed features include a simple questionnaire with text and visual cues that guide users to the existing mRS grades, a simplified layout, and an intuitive, guided user interface to reduce cognitive load and support clinical decision-making. An online survey of Canadian clinicians informed the design principles by identifying current challenges in mRS administration.
Results: Survey responses revealed consistent issues with the current mRS, including subjective interpretation and inconsistent scoring. These findings directly informed the proposed design principles of an mRS CAT, focusing on usability, efficiency, standardization and accessibility.
Conclusions: Developing a standardized CAT for the mRS represents a meaningful step toward improving the accuracy, consistency, and clinical utility of stroke disability assessments. Future work will focus on tool development, real-world validation with stakeholders, and exploration of self- or caregiver-completed versions to expand access and improve firsthand data collection during stroke recovery.

In Nova Scotia, patients with a suspected ischemic stroke are bypassed to one of 9 Primary Stroke Centres (PSC) across the province that provide thrombolysis and one Comprehensive Stroke Centre (CSC) that provides Endovascular Treatment (EVT) and thrombolysis. EVT candidates presenting at a PSC are transferred to the CSC via ground or air transport; however, delays can lead to futile transfers where patients become ineligible for EVT on arrival and may experience worse outcomes. This study has two objectives: (1) Compare outcomes between EVT candidates who present directly at the CSC versus those transferred from PSCs, and (2) Compare outcomes between ground and air transfers.
Methods: A retrospective cohort study will analyze provincial stroke and EMS registry data from 2018–2024. Logistic regression will be used to evaluate differences in functional outcomes (mRS 0–2 at discharge), adjusting for age, sex, NIHSS, comorbidities, and transfer metrics.

Conclusions: This research will identify disparities in access and outcomes, inform transfer protocols, and support evidence-based improvements to rural stroke care and emergency medical services in Nova Scotia.

AUTOMATED SMOKING CESSATION REFERRALS IN THE TIA CLINIC – INITIAL RESULTS
HEALTH SERVICES.A. Mistri1, S. Manship2, D. Eveson1
1University Hospitals Leicester NHS Trust, Stroke Medicine, Leicester, United Kingdom, 2Leicester City Council, Division Of Public Health, Leicester, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Tobacco smoking cessation is the leading preventable cause of disease and death worldwide, and smoking cessation is a key intervention for preventing vascular events. However, smoking cessation rates remain low (~15%) despite adjuncts like e-cigarettes, bupropion, varenicline and nicotine replacement therapy (NRT). This may be because people are not referred to specialist services. We piloted a new mechanism of referral to smoking cessation services from the TIA clinic.
Methods: We changed from clinician-initiated referral to automated referral to smoking support services. All current smokers attending the Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA) Clinic were referred with allowance for patient opt-out.
Results: Over 5-months, 81 referrals were sent. By the time of contact, 14/81 (17%) had already stopped smoking. 67 were still smoking. 26 accepted support, 13 declined support, and 28 were uncontactable. 4 week quit rate was 7/26 (27%), 5 continued smoking (20%), 50% were awaiting follow up, 1 was lost to follow up. Adjunct usage: NRT (13, 50%), e-cigarettes (7, 26%). None used bupropion or varenicline. Overall, short-term smoking cessation rate was high (21/81, 26%), with 14 (17%) stopping by themselves, and an additional 7 (9%) with clinic support.
Conclusions: Automated referral with opt out, after a vascular event is likely to improve success with smoking cessation, and automatic referrals should be part of a digital strategy. Additional resources to support high risk vascular clinic attendees for smoking cessation may be appropriate.. The low usage of available evidence-based medication adjuncts is surprising. Limitations of this analysis: single-centre data, short-term outcomes, and missing outcomes and medication usage data in a significant proportion.

PATIENT-DRIVEN CHRONIC REHABILITATION SERVICE AND PAYMENT STANDARD: EVIDENCE FROM POST-STROKE INPATIENTS IN SHANGHAI, CHINA
HEALTH SERVICES.Q. Qin, X. Hou, B. Zhu
Shanghai Health Development Research Center, Health Policy, Shanghai, China
Background and Aims: Rehabilitation services are critical for stroke patients, while established payments for services do not reflect patient needs. This study aims to analyze the influencing factors of post-stroke rehabilitation expenses and measure the patient-driven reimbursement rate.
Methods: Based on the data of post-stroke inpatients from five rehabilitation institutions in Shanghai (January 2021 to June 2023), the functional status and dysphagia of patients were assessed by Modified Barthel Index (MBI) and Frenchay Dysarthria Assessment (FDA), respectively, while the complications were classified into three levels under the CHS-DRG Scheme. Multiple linear regression models were used to analyze the factors influencing the logarithmsed average daily rehabilitation expenses. Furthermore, the rehabilitation services were divided into four subgroups to measure the per diem payment standard.
Results: A total of 333 post-stroke patients were enrolled using a criterion of 60 days-1 year of rehabilitation hospitalization after acute treatment. At the baseline, 70.27% patients were male, with a mean age of 62.6 years. We found that age (β=-0.0038), inpatient days (β=0.0007), MBI level (β=0.0224), FDA level (β=0.1425) and complication level (β=0.0913) had significant effects on the average daily rehabilitation expenses, resulting in a payment standard of $292 per bed day, with a reimbursement rate of 98.20%, higher than that of 52.47% associated with CHS-DRG Scheme (p<0.05).
Conclusions: Younger age, longer hospital stays, more severe MBI, FDA and comorbidities are associated with higher chronic rehabilitation fees among post-stroke inpatients. Bed-day payment calculated by patient-driven groups was more appropriate for rehabilitation services.

This study aimed to explore compassion, including the factors that enable and hinder it in virtual peer support stroke programs.

Prior to the visit there were no stroke specific guidelines or protocols in place. Current gaps and implementation priorities to achieve WSO ‘Essential Stroke Centre Certification’: formal stroke director and nurse lead/coordinator roles, occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, stroke care protocols, annual and auditable stroke training programs, 24/7 thrombolysis, and a basic stroke register. Recommendations also included staffing requirements.
Conclusions: Stroke services in PNG require additional resource investment to meet WSO certification criteria; some features can be achieved through teamwork and ongoing collaboration with overseas experts, however, some resource investment especially into staffing levels and skills will also be required. Background and Aims: Dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVF) are acquired lesions between the meningeal arteries and associated draining veins. Background and Aims: Chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH) recurrence are up to 30% after surgery. Middle meningeal artery (MMA) embolization is an effective adjunct treatment, but the optimal embolic material strategy have not been stablished yet. We compared outcomes of MMA embolization using PVA alone versus PVA plus coils after burr hole drainage for cSDH.
Methods: This study included consecutive adults undergoing burr hole drainage then MMA embolization at Centro Medico de Puerto Rico. Patients received either PVA alone (n=11) or PVA + Coils (n=12) randomly. Outcomes assessed at 3 months included reoperation, complications, and residual hematoma (>1mm, <10mm thickness on CT). Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U and Fisher’s Exact tests (p<0.05 significant).
Results: 23 patients were included (11 PVA alone, 12 PVA + Coils). Baseline characteristics including age, sex, GCS, and anticoagulant/antiplatelet use were comparable between groups (all p>0.05). No patients required reintervention (0% vs 0%). One major complication (unilateral blindness) occurred in the PVA alone group (1/11, 9.1%) versus none in the PVA + Coils group (0/12, 0%) (p>0.999). Residual hematoma rates at 3 months were similar between groups (PVA alone: 1/11, 9.1%; PVA + Coils: 1/12, 8.3%; p>0.999).
Conclusions: In this small retrospective cohort, adjunctive MMA embolization using either PVA alone or PVA combined with coils demonstrated comparable low rates of reintervention and residual hematoma at 3 months post-CSDH drainage. A single serious complication occurred with PVA alone. Due to the very limited sample size and low event rates, definitive conclusions about relative safety or efficacy cannot be drawn. Larger, prospective studies are warranted.

INDIVIDUAL PARTICIPANT DATA META-ANALYSIS OF TRANEXAMIC ACID IN INTRACEREBRAL HAEMORRHAGE
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.C. Menon1, J. Liu2, Z. Law2, C. Mutimer3, L. Woodhouse1, I. Mhlanga1, A. Polymeris4, N. Yassi3, D. Seiffge5, A. Metteroja6, S. Davis3, L. Liu2, J. Pandian7, G. Donnan8, R. Al-Shahi Salman9, P. Bath1, N. Sprigg1
1University of Nottingham, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 2Dept. of Neurology and Stroke Center Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University China National Clinical Research Center for Neurological Diseases, Neurology, Beijing, China, 3Royal Melbourne Hospital, Melbourne Brain Centre, Parkville, Australia, 4University of Basel, Basel, Switzerland, 5Insel Hospital Bern University Hospital, Bern, Switzerland, 6Helsinki University Hospital, Helsinki, Finland, 7Christian Medical College, Punjab, India, 8University of Melbourne, Victoria, Australia, 9University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Intracerebral haemorrhage(ICH) is a devastating stroke subtype with no proven haemostatic treatment. Tranexamic acid (TXA) may limit haematoma expansion by inhibiting hyperfibrinolysis. We conducted the first individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA) to evaluate the efficacy and safety of TXA.
Methods: We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, Web of Science, and WHO ICTRP (November 2024) for randomised controlled trials of intravenous TXA administered within 12 hours of ICH onset. IPD were obtained from trial investigators. A one-stage meta-analysis using generalised linear mixed models was performed. The primary outcome was 90-day functional status (modified Rankin Scale), adjusted for trial-level minimisation variables. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. The IPDMA was prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD42017054978).
Results: Five trials contributed IPD for 2,854 participants(mean age 68, female 54%). All five RCTs were low risk of bias. TXA had no significant effect on functional outcome at 90 days (aOR 1.07, 95% CI 0.93–1.23; p=0.318). TXA reduced haematoma expansion (aOR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.96; p=0.019) and day 7 mortality (aOR 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.96; p=0.027), but not mortality at 28 or 90 days. There was no increase in seizures or thromboembolic events at 90 days. No subgroup showed significant treatment interaction.
Conclusions: TXA reduces haematoma expansion and early death in ICH, but does not improve long-term functional outcomes. Given its low cost, safety, and availability, even a modest effect may justify its use as part of a bundled care approach to improve ICH outcomes. Ongoing trials will help clarify its role in clinical practice.

Background and Aims: Infections are frequent complications in patients with spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Adults aged ⩾18 years with ICH were included, excluding those with prior symptomatic infections or antibiotic use within one month before admission. First stool samples were collected after ICH onset, along with demographic and clinical data, including symptomatic respiratory or urinary bacterial infections during hospitalization. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was used to characterize the gut microbiome. Binomial regression models adjusted for age, sex, NIHSS score, and ICH volume were applied. CBM6-related carbohydrate metabolism appeared protective, while GT52 was associated with bacterial infection risk.
Conclusions: Gut dysbiosis may increase respiratory and urinary infection risk during hospitalization after ICH through enhanced microbial diversity, specific taxonomic profiles, and metabolic pathways linked to motility and carbohydrate metabolism.

MINIMALLY INVASIVE SURGERY FOR PATIENTS WITH SPONTANEOUS SUPRATENTORIAL INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.N. Aziz, S. Sattar, S. Saleem, A. Kamal
Aga Khan University and Hospital, Karachi, Pakistan
Background and Aims: Spontaneous supratentorial ICH is associated with high morbidity and mortality. MIS offers a potential alternative to conventional treatments by reducing operative trauma and improving outcomes. Recent large-scale trials have provided critical insights, allowing for more detailed comparison of MIS techniques against traditional approaches.
Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials published until July 2024 involving patients with CT-confirmed supratentorial ICH. We included all types of MIS (stereotactic and neuroendoscopic procedures) and conventional treatments (craniotomy and medical management). Primary outcome was favorable functional outcome (modified Rankin scale 0–3 or equivalent) at follow-up. Secondary outcomes included death and adverse events such as rebleeding and infection. Subgroup analyses examined the influence of age, hematoma volume, follow-up duration, functional outcome measurement tool, and timing of surgery on MIS efficacy.
Results: 23 high-quality RCTs involving 4393 patients were included. MIS was associated with improved functional outcomes compared to conventional treatments combined (OR:2.00,95%CI:1.64–2.44). When analyzed individually, MIS showed superior outcomes compared to conventional craniotomy (OR:2.10,95%CI:1.56–2.83) and medical management (OR:1.94,95%CI:1.46–2.58). Endoscopic surgery (OR:2.21,95%CI:1.59–3.06), and stereotactic techniques with thrombolysis (OR:1.97,95%CI:1.43–2.72) and without thrombolysis (OR:1.53,95%CI:1.10-2.12) also showed favorable results. For mortality, MIS exhibited lower odds (OR:0.70,95%CI: 0.57–0.86) compared to conventional treatments combined. Risk of rebleeding was lower with MIS versus craniotomy (OR:0.45,95%CI:0.28–0.72), while CNS infection rates showed no significant difference (OR:0.89,95%CI:0.50–1.58).
Conclusions: MIS is effective in improving functional outcomes and reducing mortality in supratentorial ICH. Due to heterogeneity in existing studies, further trials are needed to establish the best MIS approaches and algorithms.
EV218 / #2536
INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE IN ARTERY OF PERCHERON TERRITORY: A RARE CASE OF BILATERAL THALAMIC HEMORRHAGE
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.N. Sharma1, D. Schachter2
1All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Neurocritical Care, New Delhi, India, 2Emory University, Stroke, Atlanta, United States of America
Background and Aims: The artery of Percheron (AOP) is a rare vascular variant in which a single branch from the posterior cerebral artery supplies both paramedian thalami and the rostral midbrain. While AOP occlusion typically causes bilateral thalamic infarction characterized by altered consciousness, vertical gaze palsy, and memory impairment, hemorrhagic events are exceptionally rare and can lead to severe neurological sequelae. We present a case of bilateral thalamic hemorrhage related to AOP involvement in a patient with multiple cerebrovascular risk factors to highlight diagnostic and management challenges.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of electronic medical records for a single case, analyzing clinical presentation, radiographic data, interventions, complications, and neurological outcomes.

Results: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, chronic cerebrovascular disease, and recent cocaine use presented. Examination demonstrated vertical gaze palsy, bilateral ptosis, left hemiparesis, and NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) 2. Noncontrast CT showed bilateral medial thalamic hematomas measuring 1.8 × 1.0 × 1.2 cm (right) and 1.3 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm (left). CT angiography/venography excluded malformation or occlusion, and MRI confirmed bithalamic hemorrhages with midbrain edema extension without infarction. Hospitalization was complicated by seizures, SIADH, pneumonia, and COVID-19. By discharge, NIHSS worsened to 16 with modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 4. Repeat CT revealed hematoma expansion.
Conclusions: This case underscores the rarity and complexity of hemorrhagic AOP events, likely fueled by chronic microvascular disease and severe hypertension. Unlike ischemic presentations, hemorrhagic involvement may reflect vessel fragility from pressure surges. Early recognition, multidisciplinary management, and blood pressure control are critical. Prospective studies are needed to refine diagnostic criteria and optimize therapeutic strategies for hemorrhagic AOP syndromes.

HYPER-AI-SCAN: PROTOCOL FOR A PROSPECTIVE STUDY USING AI-ASSISTED TRANSCRANIAL SONOGRAPHY FOR EARLY DETECTION OF INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE IN ACUTE STROKE PATIENTS
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.R. Simonetti1,2, P. Canals3, J.D. Gonzalez1, M. Alanis2, D. Rodriguez Luna2
1VHIR - Vall D’Hebron Research Institute, Barcelona, Spain, 2Vall D’Hebron University Hospital, Barcelona, Spain, 3Stanford University, Radiology, Palo Alto, United States of America
Background and Aims: Intracerebral hemorrhage carries high early mortality (>40%), determined mostly by hematoma expansion within the first hours. Rapid identification is critical, yet CT imaging is often delayed or unavailable prehospital. Transcranial duplex sonography offers a non-invasive, bedside alternative, but its clinical use is limited by high operator dependence. Artificial intelligence, by automating image interpretation, offers a promising strategy to overcome this limitation and has shown strong performance in other ultrasound fields, though it has not yet been applied to TCD in ICH.
HYPER-AI-SCAN is a prospective feasibility study aiming to assess the practicality and potential diagnostic performance of an AI-assisted TCD protocol for hyperacute ICH detection. The INTERACT4 trial recently demonstrated improved outcomes with early blood pressure lowering in confirmed ICH, reinforcing the urgency of fast diagnosis.

Methods: Single-center, prospective observational feasibility study enrolling 500 acute stroke patients (<48h from onset) with a 1:4 hemorrhagic-to-ischemic ratio. Following CT confirmation, coded TCD images are acquired. Pre-trained deep learning models (CNNs and transformers) are fine-tuned to classify “ICH suspected” vs “No ICH.” Model performance will be assessed through cross-validation, focusing on sensitivity, specificity, and AUC-ROC.
Results: At the time of abstract submission, patient enrollment and data acquisition are ongoing, and no interim results are available. An interim analysis is planned and expected to be presented at the time of the conference.
Conclusions: HYPER-AI-SCAN will provide critical feasibility data on integrating AI-assisted TCD into hyperacute ICH workflows. If successful, it could enable rapid bedside triage, improve early intervention, and extend diagnostic access to prehospital and low-resource settings.

Background and Aims: Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) is a life-threatening neurological emergency commonly associated with poorly controlled hypertension. Multifocal ICH is a rarer presentation, posing diagnostic challenges and necessitating comprehensive evaluation to find the aetiology. This case report highlights the critical role of timely diagnosis and aggressive blood pressure management in mitigating the complications associated with multifocal ICH.
Methods: A 47-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of severe headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. He had a longstanding untreated hypertension. On admission, his blood pressure was critically elevated at 234/132 mmHg. CT brain revealed multiple haemorrhages in the medulla, pons, thalamus, and temporal lobe, alongside sulcal effacement. Differential diagnoses included vascular anomalies, neoplastic lesions, and inflammatory processes. CT angiography, digital subtraction angiography, CT aorta, echocardiography and blood cultures were normal. Investigations for secondary hypertension, such as plasma metanephrines, renal MRA, and vasculitis screening, were unremarkable. MRI findings supported the diagnosis of hypertensive multifocal ICH. The neuroradiology meeting concluded hypertension was the cause. Blood pressure was managed with amlodipine, ramipril, and Bendroflumethiazide.
Results: The patient responded well to antihypertensive therapy and was discharged with restored baseline mobility and no new neurological deficits. His mean 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure was 114/78 mmHg at the outpatient follow-up, and he had no new neurological deficits.
Conclusions: Multifocal ICH in the context of uncontrolled hypertension presents significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. A comprehensive evaluation is essential to exclude other causes and confirm primary hypertension as the underlying aetiology.

INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.E. Spina1, A. De Mase2, G. Servillo1, S. Barbato1, G. Leone2, M. Muto1, P. Candelaresi2, V. Andreone1

Background and Aims: Very few treatments have proven effective in reducing mortality and disability in patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), among them stroke unit care. However, In Italy, ICH patients are rarely admitted to stroke units, due to both the persistent belief that a neurosurgical environment is more appropriate and stroke unit undersizing. In this study, we retraced changes in settings of care in ICH patients at AORN Cardarelli, Naples, Italy.
Methods: All patients with a diagnosis of ICH (ICD-9-CM 431) presented to our Emergency Room between 2017-2024 were included. We analyzed the distribution over time of patients admitted from the Emergency Room to one of the four main wards dedicated to neurological emergencies (Neurology and Stroke Unit; Neurosurgery; Emergency Medicine and Intensive Care Unit (ICU)).
Results: 1957 patients were included in the analysis. Rates of ICH patients admitted to Stroke Unit progressively increased over years from 6% in 2017 to 68% in 2024. The number of patients needing ICU remained stable over time, on average 17%.
Conclusions: In our center a growing number of ICH patients are admitted to stroke unit and receive treatment from a dedicated and specifically trained medical and nursing staff. An ongoing analysis is assessing whether this different admission setting has an impact on in-hospital mortality.

TRANEXAMIC ACID FOR INTRACEREBRAL HAEMORRHAGE 3 (TICH-3): RATIONALE AND DESIGN OF A PHASE III DOUBLE BLIND RANDOMISED CONTROLLED MULTI-CENTRED SUPERIORITY TRIAL
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.C. Menon1, M. Desborough2, T. Hamilton1, R. Dineen1, T. Hepburn1, B. Dutton1, J. Newham1, S. Adegbola1, O. Mathias1, C. Cheung1, K. Cadman3, I. Roberts4, A. Montgomery5, R. Al-Shahi Salman6, C. Roffe7, D. Werring8, M. James1, P. Kelly9, K. Tobin9, T. England10, L. Woodhouse1, I. Mhlanga1, P. Bath1, N. Sprigg1
1University of Nottingham, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 2Oxford University Hospitals, Haematology, Oxford, United Kingdom, 3University of Nottingham, School Of Medicine, Stroke Trials Unit, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 4London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, United Kingdom, 5University of Nottingham, Nottingham Clinical Trials Unit, Nottingham, United Kingdom, 6University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom, 7Keele University, Keele, United Kingdom, 8National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London, United Kingdom, 9Mater University, Dublin, Ireland, 10Derby Stroke Centre, Derby, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) a medical emergency causes more than 1.7 million strokes worldwide/year with over 40% mortality. Tranexamic acid (TXA) when given early, reduces mortality and haematoma expansion in spontaneous ICH. We aim to assess the clinical effectiveness of TXA after ICH and determine whether TXA should be used in clinical practice.
Methods: TICH-3 is a pragmatic phase III prospective double-blinded randomised placebo-controlled trial. 5500 adult patients (⩾18) with spontaneous ICH (including direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) associated ICH) will be recruited within 4.5 hours of onset across UK and International sites. Exclusion criteria include known indication for TXA, contraindications for TXA, known to be on anticoagulation (except DOAC), massive ICH(>60ml), severe coma (GCS<5) and palliative care. Emergency consent will take place and patients will be randomised (1:1) by simple randomisation to receive intravenous TXA 2g; 1g bolus loading dose given as 100ml infused over 10 minutes, followed by another 1g in 250ml infused over 8hrs or matching comparator. Patients, relatives, researchers, and outcome assessors will be masked to treatment allocation. The primary outcome is mortality by day 7. Secondary outcomes include dependency (modified Rankin Score), Quality of Life at day 180, serious adverse events up to 7 days, and fatal SAEs up to day 180.
Results: As of 22nd of April 2025, 1778 (32%) participants have been recruited by 113 sites from 11 countries for the TICH-3 trial.
Conclusions: TICH-3 results will provide definitive evidence for the effectiveness of TXA. This could change clinical practice globally for a disease with few treatment options.

EV226 / #579
RATE OF HEMATOMA EXPANSION AS A PREDICTOR OF OUTCOME IN INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.K. Tran1, A. Ali2, N. Akhtar3, A. Shuaib1
1University of Alberta, Neurology, Edmonton, Canada, 2University of Toledo, Neurology, Toledo, United States of America, 3Max Rady College of Medicine, Neurology, Winnipeg, Canada
Background and Aims: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a major contributor to acute strokes, with high rates of morbidity and mortality. Although the initial hematoma volume is a well-recognized predictor of mortality in patients with ICH, little is known about hematoma expansion rate (ratio of baseline hematoma volume and time from onset to imaging acquisition) in predicting ICH patient outcomes.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients admitted with supratentorial intracerebral hemorrhage from January 2014 to December 2024. The modified Rankin Scale was dichotomized with favourable outcome (0–2) and unfavourable outcome (3–6).
Results: 1351 patients were included in the final analysis. Fast volume-expanders (>10 mL/hr) had the highest mRS score at 90 days (p=0.002) and the highest proportion of mortality at 90 days compared to slow volume expanders (<2 mL/hr) and intermediate volume expanders (2-10 mL/hr), p=0.01. Multivariate analysis revealed that age (aOR 1.01, 95% CI: 1.0001–1.03), severe stroke (NIHSS score of >10) (aOR 11.6, 95% CI: 4.64–28.9), and fast hematoma expansion rate (aOR 1.89, 95% CI: 1.10–3.28) were independent predictors of mortality at 90 days. In contrast, only age (aOR 1.04, 95% CI: 1.02–1.05), moderate stroke (aOR 2.57, 95% CI: 1.11–5.94] and severe stroke [aOR 22.3, 95% CI: 10.7–46.3) were identified as predictors of a poor outcome (mRS of 3-6) at 90 days.
Conclusions: In resource-limited settings, using a CT of the head to calculate the volume expansion rate could be a useful predictor of outcomes in patients with supratentorial ICH bleeds.
EV227 / #2394
RECURRENT CHRONIC SUBDURAL HEMATOMA DESPITE MAXIMUM-SETTING V-P SHUNT: A CASE OF OVERDRAINAGE REQUIRING SHUNT LIGATION
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.X. Wang
First Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University, Dalian, China
Background and Aims: Chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH) is a known complication of ventriculoperitoneal (V-P) shunt procedures, most often related to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) overdrainage. Although programmable valves set at high resistance are designed to minimize this risk, such complications may still occur. We present a case of recurrent CSDH in a patient with a high-pressure V-P shunt, highlighting diagnostic challenges and management considerations.
Methods: A 71-year-old man with hydrocephalus underwent V-P shunt placement via the right posterior horn, with the valve set to its highest performance level (2.5). Six months later, he developed progressive numbness of the right limbs. Cranial CT showed a left-sided CSDH. A burr hole drainage was performed, with good initial results. However, the hematoma recurred within days after the drain catheter was removed. Despite the high valve setting, overdrainage was reconsidered. The shunt’s distal catheter was ligated, followed by a second burr hole evacuation.
Results: Repeat imaging showed satisfactory resolution of the hematoma without further recurrence. Unfortunately, the patient remained unconscious postoperatively. The clinical course resembles similar cases in the literature, where high-resistance valves did not always prevent overdrainage-related subdural collections, and recurrence occurred unless CSF flow was interrupted.
Conclusions: CSDH can develop even with a V-P shunt set at maximum resistance. When hematoma recurrence follows initial drainage, shunt overdrainage should be reconsidered. Shunt ligation may be necessary to prevent reaccumulation. Delayed intervention may lead to poor neurological recovery despite radiological improvement.

Background and Aims: Fifty percent of stroke-related mortality is due to intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). After years of neutral trials and therapeutic nihilism, new findings offer hope of improved outcomes and decreased mortality for patients with ICH. Checklists are a commonly used tool that have been proven to reduce cognitive workload and errors in complex tasks. They have been used successfully in medicine and industry.
Methods: A panel of experts created a static sequential checklist based on consensus and current guidelines. A sequential checklist was chosen because some interventions (coagulopathy reversal and blood pressure lowering) are extremely time-sensitive and more beneficial when applied in the first hours after ICH.
Results: Checklist items include A) Anticoagulation Reversal, B) Blood Pressure Lowering, C) Care Setting, D) Delayed Prognostication, E) Evacuation, F) Fever Lowering, G) Glucose Management and H) Hemorrhage trials. All patients should be evaluated for anticoagulation reversal to decrease risk of hematoma expansion, receive early and steady blood pressure lowering once ICH is identified, and be triaged to a facility with a dedicated unit staffed by nurses trained to manage neurologic emergencies. Full medical support, including correction of glucose and fever abnormalities, should be provided and every patient must be evaluated for surgical intervention. Finally, ICH patients should be considered for inclusion into randomized clinical trials.
Conclusions: The ICH checklist is the first of its kind to summarize interventions proven to improve outcomes in patients with ICH. It can facilitate the dissemination of guideline-supported treatment pathways and aims to decrease disparities in care.

PLATELET MICROVESICLES ENGINEERED PT-SE AGGREGATES TREAT INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE BY RESHAPING THE IMMUNE MICROENVIRONMENT AND INHIBITING NEURONAL FERROPTOSIS
INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE.J. Zang, L. Jiang, Y. Zheng
Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital, Shanghai, China
Background and Aims: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is associated with poor prognosis due to immune hyperactivation and neuronal ferroptosis. Single-faceted therapeutic strategies often fail to address these complex pathologies, while systemic drug delivery faces challenges such as peripheral clearance and non-specific targeting. This study aimed to develop platelet-engineered PtSe aggregates (PtSe@PMV) to synergistically regulate the immune microenvironment and suppress ferroptosis, enabling targeted delivery to hemorrhagic brain regions for enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
Methods: PtSe nanoparticles were designed to combine selenium (Se)-mediated glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) synthesis for ferroptosis inhibition with platinum (Pt)-based enzyme-like activity for immune modulation. These nanoparticles were further encapsulated into platelet-derived microvesicles (PMVs) to prolong circulation and enable site-specific accumulation at hemorrhage sites. The therapeutic effects of PtSe@PMV were evaluated in preclinical ICH models, focusing on immune microenvironment remodeling, ferroptosis suppression, and neurological recovery.
Results: PtSe@PMV demonstrated enhanced brain-targeting efficiency compared to non-engineered nanoparticles, facilitating selective enrichment in the hemorrhage area. The dual-action mechanism of PtSe significantly reshaped the immune microenvironment by increasing immunosuppressive microglia populations and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Concurrently, Se-driven GPX4 upregulation mitigated lipid peroxidation and iron overload, effectively alleviating neuronal ferroptosis. These synergistic effects translated to improved neurofunctional outcomes in ICH models.
Conclusions: This study presents a novel strategy for ICH treatment by integrating enzyme-like nanomedicine with platelet-derived carriers. PtSe@PMV overcomes delivery barriers and achieves dual-pathway intervention, demonstrating remarkable potential in mitigating secondary brain injury. The findings highlight the translational promise of bioengineered nanotherapeutics for complex neurological disorders.

The aim of this study was to investigate whether the presence of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) without radiological evidence of hydrocephalus in patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) of the posterior circulation is associated with increased mortality and severe disability.
Methods: A total of 76 patients treated at the Special Hospital for Cerebrovascular Diseases "Sveti Sava" in 2022. and 2023. were analyzed. All were diagnosed with ICH based on a standardized stroke protocol. Patients were divided into two groups: one with ICH without IVH and no hydrocephalus, and another with ICH and IVH, also without hydrocephalus. Outcomes were assessed using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS), categorized as favorable (mRS 0–2) or unfavorable (mRS 3–6) and results were compared between groups using Chi-square analysis.
Results: Among 76 patients, 37 (48.7%) had ICH with IVH, and 39 (51.3%) had ICH without IVH. In the IVH group, 18.9% had favorable outcomes and 81.1% unfavorable. Conclusions: Mobilization post stroke can be achieved with low-cost interventions. Policymakers and healthcare professionals in low-resource settings are encouraged to promote post-stroke mobilization.

1University of Toronto, Medicine (neurology), Toronto, Canada, 2Toronto Western Hospital, Krembil Brain Institute, Toronto, Canada, 3Toronto Western Hospital, Medicine (neurology), Toronto, Canada
Background and Aims: Stroke-related complications require timely recognition, rapid intervention, and coordinated interdisciplinary action. The initial management of these emergencies often falls to learners and frontline nurses. However, these providers rarely have opportunities to rehearse such situations in a controlled, supervised environment. Simulation-based education (SBE) offers a high-fidelity platform for practicing real-time clinical decision-making, crisis communication, and team-based care. This study assessed whether high-fidelity stroke simulation enhanced participants’ self-perceived confidence across key domains.
Methods: Participants included nurses and trainee physicians. Simulations were conducted in a laboratory with a Gaumard Hal S5301 patient simulator. Pre- and post-simulation questionnaires were administered to assess self-perceived confidence across 15 domains using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very low, 5 = very high). Descriptive statistics were calculated, including mean scores, absolute changes, and 95% confidence intervals.
Results: Thirteen participants completed pre- and post-simulation questionnaires. All measured domains showed improvements in self-perceived confidence. The most significant gains were in managing a deteriorating patient (mean post: 4.00, change: +1.08, 95% CI: 0.73–1.43), determining appropriate investigations (mean post: 4.15, change: +1.00, 95% CI: 0.50–1.50), and escalating care (mean post: 4.31, change: +1.00, 95% CI: 0.50–1.50). Post-simulation scores ranged from 3.75 to 4.31, with the highest ratings in escalation, intervention timing, and imaging readiness.
Conclusions: SBE enhanced participants’ confidence and preparedness in managing stroke-related complications. Future iterations will incorporate clearer role assignments, structured pre-briefs, and improved scenario fidelity. The NeuroNexus initiative will expand to include new high-acuity stroke scenarios, supporting individual skill development and broader system readiness.

NONINVASIVE OR MINIMALLY INVASIVE NEUROMODULATION IN ANIMAL MODELS OF ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.I. Salles1, M. Pellegrino2, J. Kroth3, C. Dos Santos4, L. Tristao4, J. Shinosaki5, W. Bernardo4, A. Conforto6
1Hospital das Clinicas HCFMUSP, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil, 2Instituto de Radiologia, Hospital das Clinicas HCFMUPS, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil, 3Hospital Sirio Libanes, Sao Paulo, Brazil, 4Brazilian Medical Association, Department Of Evidence-based Medicine, Sao Paulo, Brazil, 5Hospital de Clinicas da Universidade Federal de Uberlandia, Uberlandia, Brazil, 6LIM-44 - Hospital das Clinicas HCFMUSP, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Sao Paulo, Sao Paulo, Brazil
Background and Aims: Neuromodulation has been investigated in both human and animal studies as a potential adjuvant therapy for rehabilitation and neuroprotection in the hyperacute phase of ischemic stroke (IS). This systematic review evaluated the neuroprotective effects of neuromodulation in animal models of IS.
Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and LILACS was conducted for in vivo preclinical studies published up to April 2024. Included studies employed non-invasive or minimally invasive neuromodulation within 24 hours of arterial occlusion and included a control group. The primary outcome was infarct size; neurological impairment, assessed by behavioral scales, was a secondary outcome. Meta-analyses for both outcomes were performed using a random-effects model in RevMan. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42020165347).
Results: Thirty studies involving 2,347 animals were included in the qualitative synthesis; 25 were eligible for meta-analysis. Most studies used middle cerebral artery occlusion models. Neuromodulation techniques included electroacupuncture (EA), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS). Across modalities, neuromodulation significantly reduced infarct size—both absolute (Figure 1) and relative (Figure 2)—and improved neurological outcomes (Figure 3). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies and interventions.

Conclusions: Preclinical evidence suggests that neuromodulation may exert neuroprotective effects following IS. Future studies should adopt standardized protocols and outcome measures to improve comparability and translational relevance.

USING COMMUNITY BASED PARTICIPATORY ACTION RESEARCH TO IDENTIFY PRIORITIES WITH YOUNG PEOPLE WITH STROKE

1Western University, Faculty Of Health Sciences, London, Canada, 2Western University, London, Canada
Background and Aims: The incidence of stroke among individuals under 65 is increasing. These People with Lived Experience of Stroke (PWLE_S) have identified balance and walking difficulties, contributing to a heightened risk of falls, as one of their top priorities. These younger PWLE_S feel that services are not tailored to them, and their experiences are underrepresented in stroke rehabilitation. The objectives of this project are to 1. Identify priorities for fall reduction in younger PWLE_S aged 30-65. 2. Co-design a knowledge mobilization strategy for actionable recommendations.
Methods: The projects and its methodology were developed with feedback from three patient advisors. Utilizing a community-based participatory action research (CBPAR) approach rooted in patient engagement principles such as co-building, inclusiveness, mutual respect and trust.. Over multiple virtual group meetings, PWLE_S meet to discuss their experiences with fall risk factors, their priorities and actionable recommendations for reducing the implications of falls and fall risk factors by sharing photos and videos.
Results: PWLE_S have identified some priorities regarding fall risk factors and its implications on different areas of life such as leisure, daily activities and work. The actionable recommendations to address these issues will focus on individual level and community level solutions. For dissemination, we will co-develop animated videos and infographics with PWLE_S.
Conclusions: The participatory nature of CBPAR facilitates collaboration with PWLE_S to identify their priorities and co-develop knowledge translation and dissemination strategies.

WORLD STROKE ORGANIZATION MECHANICAL THROMBECTOMY WORKSHOPS IMPROVE ACCESS TO MECHANICAL THROMBECTOMY IN LOW TO MIDDLE INCOME COUNTRIES
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.V. Inoa1, R. Then2, N. Cancelliere3, N. Goyal1, K. Spence4, M. Wells5, S. Martins6, G. Gordon Perue7
1Semmes Murphey Clinic, Neurology/neurosurgery, Memphis, United States of America, 2Jefferson Einstein Philadelphia Hospital, Neurology, Philadelphia, United States of America, 3St Michaels Hospital, Toronto, Canada, 4Jackson North Medical Center, Miami, United States of America, 5St. George’s University, George town, Grenada, 6Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil, 7University of Miami, Miami, United States of America
Background and Aims: Access to mechanical thrombectomy (MT) MT remains limited in low- to middle-income countries (LMICs), largely due to gaps in procedural training and system readiness. We previously demonstrated that hands-on MT workshops in the Caribbean improved procedural competency and hypothesized that this approach could be replicated in other LMICs to expand MT access.
Methods: A comprehensive 22-hour curriculum was developed, incorporating didactic sessions, hands-on simulations, and complex case studies, in collaboration with the Global Stroke Alliance in Colombia, India and Turkey from August 2022 -October 2024. The workshops were specifically designed for neurointerventional physicians and tailored to meet regional needs. Pre-course and post-course assessments evaluated physician confidence in mechanical thrombectomy (MT) procedures, while a follow-up survey at three months post-course assessed changes in MT volumes in clinical practice. Data were analyzed using summary statistics and chi-square tests.
Results: Among the 67 physicians from 16 countries who completed the MT workshops, 67% completed all pre and posttests. Physician confidence scores increased significantly from 14% pre-course to 46% post-course (P<0.005), with significant improvements in patient selection for MT (11% to 55%, P<0.005), procedural access knowledge (14% to 48%, P<0.005), thrombectomy technique (2% to 45%, P<0.005), and avoiding harmful maneuvers (2% to 39%, P<0.005). Three months after training, physicians reported a 36% rise in overall thrombectomy numbers. See Figures.

Conclusions: MT workshops that include hands-on simulation are feasible and represents a scalable pathway to expand MT access in LMIC. They are highly effective in improving MT procedural skills and confidence among neurointerventional physicians in LMICs.
EV239 / #2562
MECHANICAL THROMBECTOMY ACCESS: SURVEY OF NEUROINTERVENTIONAL WORKFORCE READINESS IN LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME COUNTRIES
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.V. Inoa1, R. Then2, N. Cancelliere3, N. Goyal1, K. Spence4, M. Wells5, S. Martins6, G. Gordon Perue7
1Semmes Murphey Clinic, Neurology/neurosurgery, Memphis, United States of America, 2Jefferson Einstein Philadelphia Hospital, Philadelphia, United States of America, 3St Michaels Hospital, Toronto, Canada, 4Jackson North Medical Center, Miami, United States of America, 5St. George’s University, George town, Grenada, 6Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil, 7University of Miami, Miami, United States of America
Background and Aims: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is a life-saving intervention for acute large vessel occlusion stroke, yet access in low- to middle-income countries (LMICs) is severely limited. Despite LMICs accounting for 87% of global stroke mortality, MT access is 88% lower than in high-income countries. While infrastructure and financing are recognized barriers, the capacity of the neurointerventional workforce has not been thoroughly assessed. We hypothesized that a trained cohort of neurointerventionalists exists in LMICs who could be upskilled to expand MT access.
Methods: A cross-sectional survey was distributed online via global stroke alliances from August 2023 to October 2024. All societies and physicians affiliated with the alliance were invited. Data from were analyzed using summary statistics.
Results: The survey identified 150 respondents across 33 LMICs (see figure 1). The majority 111/150 (74%) physicians reported formal neurointerventional training and included 39% neurosurgeons, 25% neuroradiologists, 24% interventional neurologists). Most had access to CT (91%) and CTA (88%), yet 33% of centers performed fewer than 10 MT procedures annually, 55% of physicians reported conducting less than 10 cases per year and only 2% performed more than 100 cases per year. Importantly, 93% agreed there is a need for targeted MT training to enhance their skills.

Conclusions: Despite the presence of trained specialists and basic imaging infrastructure, low procedural volumes remain a key barrier to MT scalability in LMICs. Focused skill development, particularly through targeted training and proctoring, could bridge this gap. This survey identifies an actionable cohort for immediate upskilling, providing a roadmap to improve MT access in LMICs.
EV240 / #2382
BARRIERS TO INTEGRATING TECHNOLOGY-ENABLED STROKE CARE WITHIN THE HEALTH SYSTEMS. RESULTS FROM THE PROCESS EVALUATION OF A STROKE TRIAL IN INDIA
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.S. Kamalakannan1, S. Mateti2, V. Bathina3, T. Muthuvel2, H. Pant2, S. Kinra4, H. Kuper4, M. Gvs2
1Northumbria University, Department Of Social Work, Education, And Community Wellbeing, Newcastle Upon Tyne, United Kingdom, 2Pragyaan Sustainable Health Outcomes Foundation, Hyderabad, India, 3Atharv Ability, Hyderabad, India, 4London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: A digital stroke rehabilitation intervention was systematically developed and was found feasible, acceptable, and effective in a low and middle-income country context. However, integrating and scaling up such innovative solutions within the health systems identified several barriers. Process evaluation of a randomized controlled trial in India provided in-depth insights.
Methods: A realist evaluation approach was used within the randomised clinical trial design. The objective of this approach was to identify and understand what worked, for whom, under what context, and how. Information related to support available for the stroke survivor, access to rehabilitation, costs, and scalability of the intervention was collected.
Results: reveal that there are several barriers to integrating technology-enabled stroke care within the health systems. Stroke survivors do not get therapeutic support following hospital discharge. Awareness and knowledge to support a stroke survivor were absent among informal family caregivers. Multi-disciplinary stroke care and rehabilitation services were not available to most of the participants in their community, especially within the public health infrastructure. Available services, such as physiotherapy and paid caregivers, were not affordable and were not related to the felt needs of the stroke survivors. Hospitals that treated these stroke survivors did not provide any follow-up care for these stroke survivors in the community.
Conclusions: The health system for enabling stroke care is fragmented in many countries. Innovative solutions cannot be scaled up even if its found feasible, acceptable, and effective. Integrating the scalable solution within the health systems is of immense public health importance and a global priority.
EV241 / #1605
AUDIT ON THE ASSESSMENT OF THE CARE FOR PATIENTS WITH MALIGNANT MIDDLE CEREBRAL ARTERY (MCA) SYNDROME IN A TERTIARY HOSPITAL
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.J. Kamara1,2, W.J. Liu3, R. Marigold3, M. Monsuru-Oke4, M. Ahmed3,5, E. Haq3
1University Hospital Southampton, Neurosciences, Stroke, Southampton, United Kingdom, 2Queen Alexandra Hospital, Portsmouth University Hospitals, NHS Trust, Older Peoples Medicine, Stroke, Portsmouth, United Kingdom, 3University Hospital Southampton, Southampton, United Kingdom, 4Whipps Cross University Hospital, London, United Kingdom, 5Ain Shams University, Cairo, Neurology, Faculty Of Medicine, Cairo, Egypt
Background and Aims: Malignant middle cerebral artery(MCA) syndrome carries a high mortality rate of up to 80%. If done within 48 hours of the diagnosis, decompressive surgery reduces mortality and increases the chance of a favourable outcome for patients with this condition. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends that patients with large MCA infarction should be considered for decompressive surgery. The audit aimed to assess whether NICE and local hospital guidelines were followed when caring for these patients in a hyperacute stroke unit in a tertiary neuro-surgical centre.
Methods: Adults aged 18 years and over admitted to a tertiary hospital in the UK, with the diagnosis of malignant MCA syndrome, were included in the audit. The audit was done against the local Malignant MCA protocol and NICE recommendation. It was a retrospective data collection from January 2019 to January 2024. Patients still in the hospital at the time of data collection and those with infarcts involving the ACA or PCA territories only were omitted.
Results: Only 62% of staff in HASU had good knowledge of the optimal time for decompressive craniectomy. 50% of patients had hourly MRASS and GCS monitoring as per protocol. 53% of patients had daily CT in the first 72 hours. Aspirin was held in 50% of patients on the malignant MCA watch.
Conclusions: Recommendation: Malignant MCA daily review sheet for the first 72 hours. Educate resident doctors and nurses working on HASU. Implement online stroke referral to neurosurgeons for malignant MCA patients to keep track of timing.

Methods: The barrier identified was that the stroke team included advanced clinical practitioners, medical residents and hospitalists who were new to practice and were unaware of the standards regarding the inclusion of cardio protective medications in the discharge regimens of ischemic stroke diabetes patients. Education was indicated. Monthly ACP Journal Club Presentations/Reviews of Updated Endocrine Guidelines, Mandatory Diabetes Topics, Stroke Resident Orientation and Education as well as Nurse Specific in-services (on Therapeutic Lifestyle modifications and recommendation documentation) were implemented.
Results: A formative evaluation has proven this education intervention to be successful. Conclusions: There are many barriers to optimum patient outcomes. There is the ever judgmental “non-compliance”. Education is key;but not just patient education. Provider education is crucial as well. This latter (to include clinical practice as well as an understanding of the social determinants of health) will engender successful patient outcomes. Ongoing student, multidisciplinary projects in stroke/diabetes mellitus patients are warranted and implemented.

INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITIES OF PRACTICE - ONE APPROACH TO IMPROVING STROKE CARE IN LMIC COUNTRIES: THE INDONESIA EXPERIENCE
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.G. Cumberbatch1, D. Lowe2, L. Clark3
1St George’s University NHS Foundation Trust, London, United Kingdom, 2Wirral University Teaching Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Stroke Services, Department Of Medicine For Older People, Wirral, United Kingdom, 3Dorset County Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Dorset, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Stroke is the largest cause of mortality in Indonesia (WSO 2021). As part of a 2 year programme funded by the Foreign and Commonwealth Development Office, Jakarta and in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, Indonesia and NHS England, Global Health Unit: three virtual communities of practice were established for stroke doctors, nurses and therapists from 2 regions (Jakarta and South Sumatra). Communities of practice (COP) can facilitate the sharing of knowledge and learning by drawing together groups of staff with common interests to share best practice and collaboratively solve problems.
Methods: COP groups operated virtually each month for 6 months with interpreter support and engaged staff across hospital levels and stroke care experience. Results were obtained from participant feedback, in-country presentations and collaborative engagement.
Results: 74 participants attended (32 nurses, 26 therapists, 16 doctors) over 23.5 hours. Communities of practice facilitated quality improvement projects in Indonesia including improving stroke recognition in primary care, reducing the use of urinary catheters, improving patient and carer education and primary care rehabilitation. Challenges encountered were: time differences, release of staff from clinical commitments, creating shared purpose for staff from a wide range of experience and pathways.
Conclusions: In global health arenas virtual communities of practice can provide a valuable opportunity for stroke specialist staff to collaborate, share best practice and drive in-country quality improvement strategies. Support from International colleagues can facilitate shared learning. The continuation of COPs in Indonesia could further drive stroke care improvement and extend to other regions of Indonesia.

Background and Aims: Similar to many low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), the barriers limiting wider mechanical thrombectomy (MT) access in Georgia are largely unknown. Recently, MT access score (MTAS) was introduced as a new tool for identifying and characterizing barriers to MT access. This study aimed to implement the MTAS in Georgia, a small, middle-income country, to assess and characterize national barriers to MT.
Methods: We applied the MTAS, which comprises 12 weighted attributes, each scored on a 0–3 scale, resulting in a total score range of 0–36, being 0 the worst possible score. Eight members of Mission Thrombectomy regional committee members from different regions of Georgia were invited as panelists in this survey. Four panel members are neurosurgeons from major thrombectomy-capable centers who perform more than 80% of MT in Georgia, while the remaining panelists are experienced vascular neurologists. The nominal group consensus method was used to finalize agreement among panelists for each attribute of MTAS.
Results: The total MTAS for Georgia was 17/36. The lowest score 0 was documented for two attributes: lack of prehospital LVO-specific screening and tele-stroke networks, while the highest MTAS of 3 was documented for EMS utilization.
Conclusions: MTAS is a valid tool for quantitatively assessing barriers to MT in Georgia. It identified a lack of information and the presence of physical barriers as major challenges. These findings underscore the need for targeted interventions through national stroke public health initiatives to improve access to MT.

PHASED STRATEGY FOR DIGITAL STROKE PREVENTION IN VIETNAM: LOCALISATION, VALIDATION, AND POPULATION-LEVEL IMPLEMENTATION
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.B. Nair, M. Kravchenko, V. Feigin
Auckland University of Technology, National Institute For Stroke And Applied Neurosciences (nisan), Auckland, New Zealand
Background and Aims: Vietnam has one of the highest stroke burdens globally, with over 200,000 cases annually and a rising incidence among younger populations. Environmental factors, limited preventive infrastructure, and regional inequities exacerbate this challenge. This programme aims to implement a digital stroke prevention strategy using the globally validated platforms through a three-phase approach: technology localisation, a secondary prevention clinical trial, and a primary prevention pilot at the community level.
Methods: In the first stage, the digital tools (such as Stroke Riskometer and Prevents-MD) will be localised for Vietnamese users, including interface translation, cultural adaptation, and API deployment. The second stage involved a single-centre, 12-month secondary prevention trial at a tertiary stroke centre in Hanoi involving 360 stroke survivors, assessing digital engagement, adherence, and environmental risk contexts (e.g., Agent Orange exposure). The last stage involved a community-based pilot enrolling 10,000 adults, with 1,000 high-risk individuals followed for 12 months. The digital algorithm will also be optimised using retrospective ACVD >10% data.
Results: We expect improved patient engagement, lifestyle change, and reduced recurrence in the secondary prevention cohort, alongside community uptake and digital feasibility. Differential uptake across rural vs. urban settings may highlight underlying digital access and literacy gaps, informing future health equity strategies.
Conclusions: Combining clinical validation, implementation science, and equity-driven outreach, it offers a blueprint for LMICs seeking to address stroke and non-communicable diseases through technology-enabled care. By aligning algorithms with local infrastructure and regulatory frameworks, the programme establishes a pathway for responsible digital adoption while protecting intellectual property and long-term sustainability in cross-national partnerships.

NIGHTTIME INTERRUPTIONS AND HOSPITAL ACQUIRED DELIRIUM AMONG OLDER PATIENTS WITH ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE: ANALYSIS OF CLINICAL WORKFLOW IMPACTS ON PATIENT RESTFULNESS AND OUTCOMES
IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.A. Pan1, T. Potter1, K. Agarwal2, S. Nowakowski3, J. Meers3, K. Borei4, C. Bruce2, G. Taffet2, F. Vahidy5
1Houston Methodist, Center For Health Data Science & Analytics, Houston, United States of America, 2Houston Methodist, Houston, United States of America, 3Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, United States of America, 4Houston Methodist, Department Of Neurosurgery, Houston, United States of America, 5TIRR Memorial Hermann, Houston, United States of America
Background and Aims: Hospital restfulness is increasingly recognized as a patient-centered goal. We evaluated how clinical workflow-related nighttime interruptions impact hospital acquired delirium (HAD) and discharge outcomes among acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients.
Methods: We analyzed AIS patients aged ⩾70 years across 7 stroke-certified hospitals (Jan 2018 – Apr 2025). Inclusion criteria were absence of delirium on admission and ⩾ 2 nights of hospital stay. Nighttime (10PM to 5AM) interruptions were extracted from EMR entries related to records related to imaging, laboratory, medication, vitals, bathing. A restful night was defined as ⩾ 4 uninterrupted hours. Overall restfulness was categorized as high (>75% restful nights), moderate (50-75%), or low (<50%). Outcomes included HAD (12-hour 4AT assessments) and unfavorable discharge (skilled nursing and long-term care). Associations between nighttime interruptions and outcomes were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression (adjusting for pertinent stroke features). Adjusted odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) are reported.
Results: Among 10,779 AIS patients, 3,830 met criteria (median age: 77.0 years; 54.6% female; median length of stay: 4.0 days). Over 60% experienced low restfulness, among whom 21.8% developed HAD (Table 1). Compared to high restfulness, those experiencing low restfulness had a nearly 3-fold independently higher odds of HAD (aOR: 2.85, CI: 1.93-4.36) and nearly 4-fold higher odds of unfavorable discharge (aOR: 3.98, CI: 2.55-6.54) (Figure 1).

Conclusions: Nighttime interruptions are significantly associated with delirium and poor discharge outcomes. Optimizing overnight clinical workflows may improve post stroke-stroke recovery trajectories.

IMPLEMENTATION & KNOWLEDGE TRANSLATION.J. Rivillas1, P. Amaya1, T. Álvarez2, C. Jimenez Monsalve3, Á. Vallejo4, M. Cardozo5, Á. Corredor6, E. González3, N. Llanos-Leyton7, D. Manrique8, B. Pabon9, H. Bayona3, L. Carbonera10
1Fundación Valle del Lili Hospital Universitario, Cali, Colombia, 2Hospital Internacional de Colombia, Bucaramanga, Colombia, 3Hospital Simón Bolívar, Bogotá, Colombia, 4Hospital Departamental de Nariño, Pasto, Colombia, 5Angiosur, Medellin, Colombia, 6Clinica Central del Quindio, Armenia, Colombia, 7Universidad Icesi, Neurology, Cali, Colombia, 8Clinica Shaio, Bogotá, Colombia, 9ANGIOTEAM, Director, Medellin, Colombia, 10Hospital Moinhos de Vento, Neurology And Neurosurgery, Porto Alegre, Brazil
Background and Aims: Timely access to acute stroke treatment remains uneven across many countries, including Colombia, where geographic, infrastructural, and systemic barriers limit access to reperfusion treatment. MAPSTROKE is a computational strategy developed in Brazil to analyse access to reperfusion therapies and support data-driven implementation of stroke centers.
Methods: Hospitals with acute reperfusion protocols were defined as acute stroke centers (ASCs). Hospitals with a CT scanner and an emergency department open 24/7 were categorized as potential acute stroke centres (PASCS). The MAPSTROKE calculated stroke care coverage with all ASCs and PASCs added, adding artificial points (APs) where no hospital existed, to a goal of 90% of coverage and a maximum range of 45 minutes in road transport time. Roadmaps and demographic data were obtained from the OpenStreetMaps© database and the Meta© Data for Good initiative.
Results: Approximately 67% of the Colombian population is within 45 minutes of any of the 181 existing ASCs. By creating 23 stroke centers from the list of 135 PASCs provided, this coverage would reach around 77%. After the designation of 52 APs in space for creating new stroke centers, the coverage would reach up to 88%. From this point on, adding one AP would increase the coverage by less than 0.1%.

Conclusions: The MAPSTROKE provided a framework for establishing stroke centers in the National Stroke Plan in Colombia. However, its solution may be challenging in regions with complex geography or low demographic density, which demands new solutions, such as telestroke spokes or alternative means of transportation.

Background and Aims: Vertigo is a prevalent and diagnostically challenging presentation in emergency departments, often requiring precise differentiation between central and peripheral causes. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of a simulation-based educational (SBE) workshop in enhancing residents’ knowledge, confidence, and clinical approach in managing vertigo across Emergency Medicine, Neurology, and ENT specialties.
Methods: A pre-post intervention study was conducted among 65 residents at Hamad General Hospital. LARGE ARTERY DISEASE.I. Ben Kraiem1, N. Bouattour2,3, N. Charfi3, K. Moalla2, S. Daoud3, S. Sakka2, M. Damak2
1University hospital of Sfax, Tunisia, Neurology Department, Sfax, Tunisia, 2Habib Bourguiba University Hospital, Sfax, Tunisia, Neurology, sfax, Tunisia, 3Faculty of medecine Sfax Tunisia, Departement Of Adult Neurology Habib Bourguiba, Sfax, Tunisia

NEUROCRITICAL CARE.N. Aderinto1, Y. Ajayi2, G. Olatunji3, E. Kokori3, A. Babalola4, O. Asifat5, I. Abraham3, E. Ogungbemi6, P. Bolaji7
1LADOKE AKINTOLA UNIVERSITY OF TECHNOLOGY, Ogbomoso, Nigeria, 2College of Health Sciences, Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Nigeria, 3³Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Ilorin, Ilorin, Nigeria, 4Faculty of Dentistry, College of Medicine, University of Ibadan, Ibadan, Nigeria, 5Georgia Southern University, Georgia, United States of America, 6Rostov State Medical University, Rostov-on-Don, Russian Federation, 7Dorset County Hospital NHS Foundation Trust UK, Dorchester, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Stroke, a leading cause of death and disability globally, lacks consistent neuroprotective therapies. Intravenous magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) is a candidate due to its neuroprotective properties, yet clinical efficacy remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates MgSO4’s effectiveness and safety in acute stroke.
Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines [CRD420250652637], we searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing intravenous MgSO4 in acute stroke. Outcomes included functional recovery (e.g., modified Rankin Scale), mortality, and adverse events. Data were pooled using random-effects models, with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) calculated. Heterogeneity was assessed via I² statistics.

Results: Eighty acute stroke (sixty-four ischemic and sixteen hemorrhagic) patients were enrolled (twenty in each treatment arm). Compared with group-1, the mean serum Cl concentrations were significantly lower in other groups at day-1 and day-2 with lowest observed in group 4. The highest proportion of mRS 0-2 subjects was seen in patients randomized to Nacl: Na-acetate 2:1 ratio at 30- and 90-days post randomization.
Conclusions: IV NaCl- NaOAc combination fluids were effective in reducing serum Cl concentrations in a dose dependent manner compared with IV NaCl without any increase in safety events in acute stroke patients. The therapeutic potential of IV NaCl- NaOAc combination should be further evaluated in larger randomized clinical trials in acute stroke patients.
