UNCOVERING TRANSIENT GLOBAL AMNESIA IN ACUTE STROKE UNITS. A CASE SERIES WITH SUPPORTIVE MRI EVIDENCE
NEUROIMAGING.K.R. Ng, G. Yiin, R. Heng, C. Chan
National Neuroscience Institute, Singapore, Singapore
Background and Aims: Transient global amnesia (TGA) is a clinical syndrome which classically features acute anterograde amnesia as its major symptom. With an acute presentation of symptoms such as confusion, disorganisation and perserveration, cerebrovascular event is a possible differential that would be heavily considered. This case series aims to present on patients who were admitted to an acute stroke unit, with MRI findings to highlight the potential mimicry that such a condition plays in stroke management.
Methods: Our cases largely revolve around patients with presentation of an acute anterograde amnesia, coupled with other symptoms including that of vomiting, nausea, and occasional paraesthesia. Examples include our first case who presented with acute anterograde amnesia, coupled with word repetition. Functionally, patient was still able to drive. This episode lasted for approximately 8 hours with no further memory impairment after.
Results: In the above cases, there was DWI hyperintensity with corresponding ADC hypointensity present in the right hippocampus. These findings were suggested to be attributed to transient global amnesia.

Conclusions: Through this case series, we aim to highlight the prevalence of various stroke mimic presentations. While TGA is largely a clinical diagnosis, the use of MRI modality provides a unique narrative to the case series. With the increased recognition of stroke-like symptoms, there should also be a corresponding increase in the differentiation and ability to exclude stroke mimics.
EV296 / #1095
PICTORIAL REVIEW ON MRI VESSEL WALL IMAGING FOR STROKE ASSESSMENT
NEUROIMAGING.L. Nirwan1, H. Jain2, A. Bansod3, T. Patil4, S. Sriwastava5, A. Deshmukh6
1Tesla Imaging & Intervention, Department Of Radiology, Nagpur, India, 2tesla imaging, Radiology, nagpur, India, 3Super Speciality Hospital and Govt. Medical College, Neurology, Nagpur, India, 4Jawaharlal Nehru Medical College, Datta Meghe Institute of Higher Education and Research,Sawangi, Neurology, Wardha, India, 5The University of Texas Health Science Center, Houstan, Radiology, Houston, United States of America, 6Northen Ontario School of Medicine, Sudbury, Canada
Background and Aims: Stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) vessel wall imaging (VWI) is an advanced modality offering detailed visualization of intracranial and extracranial vasculature. This pictorial aims to highlight its diagnostic value and enable readers to plan MRI studies, optimal sequences, interpret vessel wall MRI, identify stenosis, assess vascular remodeling, recognize and characterize plaques, identify underlying disease and helps in treatment.
Methods: We evaluated MRI VWI protocols, emphasizing high-resolution T1-weighted, T2-weighted, blood flow suppression black blood sequence, 3D isotropic imaging and contrast-enhanced sequences for vessel wall assessment. Imaging data from stroke patients were analyzed to depict pathologies, including atherosclerosis, vasculitis, dissection, and moyamoya disease. Annotated images highlighted plaque characteristics including stable and unstable plaque, wall thickening, stenosis cause, remodeling and contrast enhancement pattern.
Results: MRI VWI excelled in visualizing vessel wall abnormalities. Atherosclerosis showed eccentric thickening with lipid core, intraplaque hemorrhage, fibrous cap, plaque ulceration, thrombus, varied contrast uptake, vasculitis displayed concentric thickening with enhancement, dissections revealed intramural hematomas, and moyamoya exhibited narrowing with collaterals. The modality enabled precise plaque characterization, disease identification, and remodeling assessment, providing critical insights for treatment planning.
Conclusions: MRI VWI is a cutting-edge tool in stroke assessment, extending beyond stenosis detection to characterize plaques, identify diseases, evaluate remodeling, and guide treatment strategies. This pictorial review empowers readers to plan MRI vessel wall studies, choose sequences, and interpret findings, assisting physicians in diagnoses and helps in stroke care.
EV297 / #1148
ASSOCIATION OF MINIMAL CLINICALLY IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE (MCID) WITH INFARCT VOLUME IN CLINICAL POST-STROKE OUTCOMES
NEUROIMAGING.U. Pensato1, J. Ospel2, J. Zhang2, K. Barakhanov2, K. Tanaka2, F. Bala3, C. Kaveeta2, D. Kim2, M. Shamy4, M. Horn2, T. Field5, B. Buck6, A. Tkach7, L. Catanese8, R. Swartz9, T. Sajobi2, M. Almekhlafi10, A. Demchuck11, B. Menon2, A. Ganesh10, N. Singh12
1Humanitas University, Milan, Italy, 2University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada, 3University Hospital of Tours, Tours, France, 4The Ottawa Hospital, Ottawa, Canada, 5University of British Columbia, Neurology, Vancouver, Canada, 6University of Alberta, Edmonton, Canada, 7Interior Health, Kelowna, Canada, 8Hamilton Health Sciences Regional Rehabilitation Center, Hamilton, Canada, 9University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada, 10University of Calgary, Dept Of Neuroclinical Sciences, calgary, Canada, 11University of Calgary, Department Of Clinical Neurosciences, Calgary, Canada, 12University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada
Background and Aims: We aimed to evaluate the follow-up infarct volume (FIV) reduction corresponding to 1%, 5%, and 10% changes in functional outcomes in acute ischemic stroke treated with intravenous thrombolysis (IVT).
Methods: Data are from the AcT trial (Alteplase vs. Tenecteplase in AIS within 4.5 hours). Patients with available 24-hour infarct volume segmentations were included. The primary outcome was mRS=0-1. Associations between outcomes and FIV were investigated with regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, onset-to-imaging time, and hemorrhagic transformation. Sensitivity analyses were performed for patients with NCCT alone vs. MRI follow-up imaging and patients treated with EVT vs. those not treated with EVT.
Results: 1478 patients were included (median age 74 years [IQR=63-83], 713 [48.2%] females). Median FIV was 2.7 mL (IQR=0-18.2), and 527 (35.7%) achieved mRS=0-1. There was a significant association between FIV and mRS=0-1: adjusted odds ratio 0.96 (95%CI=0.96-0.97) per 1-mL FIV increase. The median delta FIV associated with a 1%, 5%, and 10% increase in the adjusted probability of achieving excellent functional outcomes were 1.2 mL (IQR=1.1-1.4), 6.0 mL (IQR=5.7-7.0), and 11.9 mL (IQR=11.3-13.7), respectively. Among patients investigated with MRI rather than NCCT, slightly smaller infarct volume reductions were required to achieve better functional outcomes, whereas no difference in this relationship was observed in patients treated with EVT compared to those who were not.

Conclusions: In acute ischemic stroke patients treated with IVT, a reduction of ~1 mL, ~6 mL, and ~12 mL in FIV corresponded to a 1%, 5%, and 10% increase in the absolute probability of achieving excellent function outcomes.
EV298 / #1859
ULTRASONIC EVALUATION OF ARTERIAL STENOSIS IN ACUTE STROKE PATIENTS
NEUROIMAGING.M. Pradeep, S. Lakshmi, D. Embramadathil
Eumed Super Speciality Hospital, Stroke & Neurovascular Sonology, Palakkad, Kerala, India
Background and Aims: The intracranial arterial stenosis are common findings of stroke patients in Asia. We reviewed our stroke database to investigate clinical factors related to intracranial arterial stenosis, including carotid disease, and peripheral arterial disease which reflects advanced atherosclerosis
Methods: Stroke patients who visited our from March 2016 to March 2024 were investigated non invasively with Power M Mode Trans cranial doppler (TCD )studies and carotid & vertebral artery duplex ultrasonography.
Results: The total number of 1984 patients were included for analysis. Three groups of intracranial arterial stenosis are defined according to TCD criteria: no vessel stenosis is in about 30% of the patients.Stenosis involving 1-2 vessels were seen in 44% of patients, stenosis involving more than 3 vessels were seen in 26%. The common and internal carotid arteries were examined using duplex ultrasonography, and the largest diameter of plaques & doppler sdpectra were recorded. Carotid arterial plaques are defined into 3 groups: diameter smaller than 2mm is 40%, diameter between 2-4mm ix 30% and diameter larger than 4mm is 20%. As the number of intracranial artery stenosis increases, the prevalence of carotid arterial plaque with moderate degree or severe degree also has increased accordingly.
Conclusions: Among acute stroke patients, more than a half of them have intracranial arterial stenosis to some extent. These patients are also more likely to have atherosclerosis as revealed by a higher incidence of plaques of moderate to large sizes in carotid arteries.
EV299 / #972
ACUTE TRANSVERSE INFARCTION OF THE LOWER SPINAL CORD AND CONUS MEDULLARIS: A CASE REPORT
NEUROIMAGING.A. Rajaratnam, B. Senanayake
Institute of Neurology, National Hospital Of Sri Lanka, Colombo, Sri Lanka
Background and Aims: Acute paraparesis with sphincter dysfunction often suggests a vascular aetiology. Spinal cord infarctions are typically localised to anterior or posterior vascular territories, making pansensory loss uncommon.
Methods: Case: A 45-year-old female with diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia developed sudden pelvic pain followed by paraplegia, urinary retention, and constipation while reaching upward from a bent position. On examination, she had flaccid bilateral lower limb paralysis (0/5), areflexia, positive Babinski sign, a positive Beevor sign, and a T10 sensory level for all modalities. Cranial nerves, fundi, and upper limbs were normal. Vitals were stable with palpable distal pulses. MRI spine revealed T2-FLAIR hyperintensity extending from the anterior D9 cord to a complete transverse involvement from D11 to the conus medullaris, without diffusion restriction or contrast enhancement (Figure). Digital subtraction angiography showed a normal thoracic aorta and spinal vasculature. Blood investigations, ANA, CSF, thrombophilia screen, echocardiogram, and Holter monitoring were unremarkable. Initially treated as myelitis with intravenous methylprednisolone without improvement, she was subsequently managed with antiplatelets and statins. Despite rehabilitation, she remained wheelchair-bound with intermittent catheterisation at one year. Repeat MRI showed atrophy of the affected segments.

Results: Discussion: Extensive transverse infarction involving the conus medullaris is rare and associated with poor outcomes. Postural arterial insufficiency or embolic phenomena may have contributed in this case.
Conclusions: This case illustrates the clinical and radiological features of a rare, extensive lower spinal cord infarction involving the conus, highlighting its devastating prognosis.
EV300 / #874
CONTRALATERAL FACIOLINGUAL HEMIPLEGIA SECONDARY TO CORTICAL AND CAPSULAR INFARCTS: A CASE BASED COMPARISON
NEUROIMAGING.A. Rajaratnam, B. Senanayake, A. Fernando
Institute of Neurology, National Hospital Of Sri Lanka, Colombo, Sri Lanka
Background and Aims: Linguofacial Hemiplegia, the combination of unilateral facial, tongue and arm weakness, is a rare stroke syndrome.
Methods: Case 1: A 57-year-old male, smoker with ischaemic heart disease and dyslipidaemia, presented with acute right lower facial weakness, aphasia, tongue deviation to the right, and right arm drift (NIHSS 5). Alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) was given at 2 hours from onset. Initial NCCT was normal; MRI showed an acute infarct in the left premotor cortex (face–tongue–hand area; Figure 1A). Holter monitoring revealed paroxysmal atrial arrhythmia, and Rivaroxaban was commenced. Case 2: A 42-year-old male with smoking, dyslipidaemia, and left carotid stenosis (80%) presented with acute right lower facial weakness, lingual dysarthria, tongue deviation to the right, and dense arm weakness (NIHSS 8). Tenectaplase (0.25 mg/kg) was given at 2 hours from onset. Initial NCCT was normal; Repeat NCCT at 24 hours revealed an acute infarct in the genu of the left internal capsule (Figure 1B). Early carotid endarterectomy was considered.

Results: Discussion: Both had contralateral pyramidal faciolingual-arm weakness with preserved palate and leg function. Cortical infarct caused severe aphasia with mild limb weakness; capsular infarct led to marked arm paresis with mild dysarthria. Both tolerated oral feeds, received antiplatelets, statins, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and showed good functional outcome by 1 month. Faciolingual hemiplegia classically localizes to the internal capsule, though cortical causes are rare.
Conclusions: Strokes of the genu of the internal capsule or the premotor cortex can result in contralateral faciolinguo hemiplegia, and show subtle clinical differences.
EV301 / #1838
PREVALENCE AND PROGNOSTIC SIGNIFICANCE OF COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY MARKERS OF HEMATOMA ENLARGEMENT IN INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE
NEUROIMAGING.F.A. Rakotomavo, R. Andriamalala, M. Ratojoniaina, N. Raveloson
Joseph Raseta Befelatanana, Intensive Care Unit, Antananarivo, Madagascar
Background and Aims: Hematoma expansion is observed in almost one-third of patients with hemorrhagic stroke, and it is mainly occurs within the first hours of evolution. Some computed tomography markers were identified as predictive of hematoma enlargement. Our study aims to determine the prevalence of those computed tomography markers of hematoma enlargement and to evaluate the influence of their presence on the outcome of patients.
Methods: This was a prospective, multicenter, descriptive and analytical cohort study of patients with intracerebral hemorrhage hospitalized in the emergency, intensive care, neurosurgery and medical departments of five hospitals of Antananarivo, from June 2021 to December 2021.
Results: One hundred patients were included in our study. The initial hematoma was large in 38% of cases. The prevalence of computed tomography markers of hematoma enlargement was 43%. The island sign (15%) was the most frequent. The median BAT score was 0 [0-4]. The blend sign (RR, 21.22; 95% CI, 1.7-256.4; p=0.016) and the satellite sign (RR, 35.71; 95% CI, 3.4-369.4; p=0.002) were found as an independent risk factor for neurological deterioration. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predicting value for predicting poor outcome were 66.6%, 94.2%, 33.3% and 70.2% for the blend sign and 26.6%, 94.2%, 66.6% and 75% for the satellite sign. The independent risk factor for mortality was the ICH score (RR, 3.38; 95% CI, 1.2-9.1; p=0.015). The Glasgow coma scale was a protective factor (RR, 0.63; 95CI, 0.4-0.8; p<0.001).
Conclusions: The blend sign and the satellite sign are independent predictors of neurological deterioration with good reliability.
EV302 / #1923
PSEUDO SUBARACHNOID HAEMORRHAGE – A RADIOLOGICAL FINDING IN A CASE OF MENINGITIS PRESENTING AS AN ACUTE STROKE
NEUROIMAGING.O. Ramdin, D. Mcgranaghan, M. Ford, J. Mcilmoyle
Royal Victoria Hospital, Stroke Medicine, Belfast, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Community acquired bacterial meningitis (CABM) has a substantial morbidity and mortality. One adverse effect of CABM is stroke (13.09%) – which is an independent predictor of poor clinical outcome (46% mortality; 62% morbidity). Potential pathologies for stroke in the setting of CABM include vasospasm and inflammatory vasculitis. Contrast extravasation, presenting as hyperdensity on commuted tomography(CT) of the head, is often reported as subarachnoid haemorrhage. This case demonstrates that meningitis need to be considered as a differential diagnosis in an unwell patient presenting as an acute stroke, with CT head showing hyperdensity following contract injection.
Methods: 48-year-old female presented within the lysis window following acute onset of left sided weakness; NIHSS 15. She described a gradual onset of headache. Initial Computed Tomography(CT) of the brain and intracranial angiography demonstrated no acute change; hence thrombolysis was administered with consent. Due to agitation, a repeat CT brain was performed which showed high density material within the sylvian fissures - reported as subarachnoid haemorrhage(SAH). Over the next day, she became increasingly drowsy with raised inflammatory markers. An infective cause was suspected. Preliminary results of lumbar puncture were in keeping with bacterial infection and empirical antibiotic therapy was commenced.
Results: Magnetic resonance imaging of the head confirmed acute infarction in the right internal capsule, but no evidence of bleeding on susceptibility weighted imaging sequence. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grew Neisseria Meningitidis.
Conclusions: Contrast extravasation mimics SAH on a plain CT head post contrast exposure. In an unwell patient presenting with an acute stroke, meningitis is an important differential diagnosis.
EV303 / #2589
DENTATE NUCLEUS DILATED PERIVASCULAR SPACES ON MRI IN HYPERTENSIVE ARTERIOPATHY
NEUROIMAGING.D. Renard1, T. Parva2, A. Wacongne2, K. Yean1, L. Deasy2, S. Laurent-Chabalier1
1CHU Nîmes, Univ. Montpellier, Nîmes, France, 2CHu Nîmes, Nîmes, France
Background and Aims: On MRI, small vessel disease-related abnormalities include cerebral microbleeds (CMB), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and dilated perivascular spaces (DPVS). In the cerebellum, deep CMB/ICH involving the dentate nucleus (DN) is associated with hypertensive arteriopathy (HA), whereas superficial CMB/ICH is associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). We aimed to study DPVS inside the DN (DN-DPVS) in patients with HA or CAA and to compare both groups.
Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the presence and the number of DN-DPVS on T2-weighted 3T MRI from 29 HA and 43 CAA patients presenting with hemorrhage-related symptoms, consecutively recruited in the stroke database of our center (Nîmes University Hospital, France) between January 2015 and December 2024.
Results: On univariate analysis, compared with CAA, HA patients were younger (median age 68.5 vs. 75, p=0.015), had more frequently diabetes (24% vs. 5%, p=0.014), showed lower CMB number (median number 1 vs. 3, p=0.013), higher basal ganglia DPVS scores (p<0.001), and more frequent presence of DN-DPVS (97% vs. 63%, p<0.001). DN-DPVS number was higher in HA compared with CAA (median number 6 vs. 2, p<0.001). The multivariate model entering age, diabetes and DN-DPVS showed p-values of 0.005, 0.058, and 0.001, respectively. For analysis of predictive ability of HA, the highest area under ROC curve was observed when combining age, diabetes and DN-DPVS (AUC 0.783).
Conclusions: DN-DPVS is almost constantly observed in HA patients whereas lacking in more than one-third of CAA patients. DN-DPVS absence might be used as radiological feature with good positive predictive value for HA.
EV304 / #2353
A DEEP RESIDUAL U-NET APPROACH FOR ROBUST STROKE LESION SEGMENTATION IN DIFFUSION-WEIGHTED MRI
NEUROIMAGING.S.M. S1, S. Mdletshe1, A. Wang1,2,3,4,5,6, D.J. Lin7
1University of Auckland, Medical And Health Science, Auckland, New Zealand, 2University of Auckland, Auckland Bioengineering Institute, Auckland, New Zealand, 3University of Auckland, Centre For Brain Research, Auckland, New Zealand, 4University of Auckland, Medical Imaging Research Centre, Auckland, New Zealand, 5University of Auckland, Centre For Co-created Ageing Research, Auckland, New Zealand, 6Matai Medical Research Institute, Auckland, New Zealand, 7Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Center For Neurotechnology And Neurorecovery, Department Of Neurology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America
Background and Aims: Precise segmentation of stroke lesions from diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is essential for quantifying ischemic damage and guiding post-stroke therapeutic interventions. This study presents the development and evaluation of a 3D Residual U-Net model for automated stroke lesion segmentation, focusing on achieving high accuracy and robust generalizability across heterogeneous patient data.
Methods: The model was trained using a dataset of 105 acute stroke DWI scans. A fivefold cross-validation strategy was applied to 80 training subjects to assess intra-dataset consistency. Patch-based input sampling focused on lesion-containing regions to optimize learning efficiency. The model architecture incorporated deep residual connections and a strengthened bottleneck to enhance feature extraction. Evaluation metrics included the Dice similarity coefficient, Intersection over Union (IoU), precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the ROC curve (AUC). Generalization was tested on an independent held-out set of 25 subjects.
Results: The model demonstrated consistent cross-validation performance with Dice scores of 0.84, 0.82, 0.79, 0.84, and 0.82 across the five folds, indicating stable learning. On the held-out test set, the model achieved a Dice score of 0.8240, IoU of 0.70, precision of 0.85, recall of 0.798, F1-score of 0.82, and AUC of 0.89. These results confirm the model’s robust segmentation performance and ability to balance sensitivity and specificity.
Conclusions: The proposed 3D Residual U-Net achieves accurate and generalizable stroke lesion segmentation from DWI. Its strong performance supports its potential integration into automated neuroimaging pipelines for stroke diagnosis and clinical decision-making.
EV305 / #2551
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ADVANCED IMAGING IN NEUROVASCULAR CARE
NEUROIMAGING.N. Sharma1, D. Schachter2
1All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Neurocritical Care, New Delhi, India, 2Emory University, Stroke, Atlanta, United States of America
Background and Aims: Recent years have seen explosive growth in AI for stroke imaging and risk stratification. In aneurysm management, machine learning(ML)models show strong predictive accuracy. A 2024 systematic review(18,670 aneurysm cases)found ML algorithms achieved pooled sensitivity ~83% and specificity ~83% for predicting rupture risk. Positive likelihood ratio was 4.81 (95%CI 3.29–7.02), indicating substantial discrimination of high-risk lesions.Such performance (AUC ~0.88 in many studies)rivals traditional risk models and suggests AI could alert clinicians to dangerous aneurysms for preemptive therapy.
Methods: In acute stroke imaging, deep learning is enhancing lesion segmentation and outcome prediction. On MRI,nnU-Net models trained on DWI achieved mean infarct segmentation Dice ≈0.810 (±0.155) on internal data,vastly outperforming conventional U-Net(Dice ≈0.493±0.236, p<0.001). Performance generalized well to external cases Dice≈0.704±0.199). These highly optimized networks allow accurate volumetric analysis(e.g. 98–100% sensitivity for large infarcts). Such tools can automate core/penumbra quantification,expediting treatment decisions.
Results: AI also refines CT perfusion analysis. In a multicenter study (N=362), two automated CTP platforms(Viz.ai vs RAPID.AI)were compared.Viz.ai systematically estimated larger ischemic core(+8 cc mean)and penumbra(+18 cc) than RAPID (p<0.001). Despite these volume differences, overall eligibility for thrombectomy by DEFUSE-3 criteria did not differ significantly between platforms. This highlights that scanner protocols and software choice can influence penumbra/core estimates,underscoring the need for harmonized imaging workflows.

Conclusions: Integrating AI into neuroimaging can unlock “superhuman” analyses: from automated lesion segmentation(Dice ≈0.81)to prediction of aneurysm rupture with ~83% accuracy.These tools show excellent concordance with clinical outcomes and may improve consistency.However, careful validation is required: as seen in perfusion software comparisons,systematic biases may arise between algorithms.Ongoing research should focus on robust multicenter trials,explainability,and clinical integration to ensure these advances truly benefit patients.
EV306 / #2116
AI-BASED DIAGNOSIS OF INTRACRANIAL ARTERIAL DISEASE USING TIME-OF-FLIGHT MAGNETIC RESONANCE ANGIOGRAPHY
NEUROIMAGING.W.-K. Seo1, J.-U. Choi2, I.Y. Baek1, H.-N. Song1, J.-E. Lee1, S. Ju3, K. Kim1,3, Y.H. Ha1
1Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, Korea, Republic of, 2Urgent Inc., Seoul, Korea, Republic of, 3SAIHST, Sungkyunkwan University, Digital Health, Seoul, Korea, Republic of
Background and Aims: Advancements in artificial intelligence have enabled automated and quantitative diagnosis of neuroimaging in the field of stroke. In this study, we developed an AI-based model to diagnose intracranial arterial disease using time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA).
Methods: We analyzed data from 1,000 cerebrovascular disease-free controls and 1,000 acute stroke patients. A multi-modal transformer model was applied to classify MRA images as normal or abnormal. For abnormal images, further classification was performed to identify intracranial atherosclerosis, moyamoya disease, and reversible vasoconstriction syndrome. Model performance was validated using 5-fold and k-fold cross-validation.
Results: The model demonstrated excellent performance in distinguishing normal from abnormal images, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9977, accuracy of 0.9771, and precision of 0.9818 in 5-fold cross-validation. For detailed classification of intracranial diseases (intracranial atherosclerosis, intracranial artery dissection, reversible vasoconstriction syndrome, and moyamoya disease), the model achieved an AUC of 0.8628, accuracy of 0.6545, and precision of 0.7141.
Conclusions: AI-based diagnosis of intracranial artery disease using TOF-MRA is feasible and shows promise for clinical application.
EV307 / #1248
DUAL ENERGY CT FOR DIFFERENTIATING INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE FROM CONTRAST EXTRAVASATION AFTER ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE INTERVENTION (DECT-ICH)
NEUROIMAGING.Z. Siddiqi1, A. Alizadeh1, R. Afshar1, A. Randhawa2, A. Trivedi1, S. Alcock2, J. Shankar2
1Section of Neurology, Department of Medicine, Max Rady College of Medicine, Neurology, Winnipeg, Canada, 2Department of Radiology, Max Rady College of Medicine, Winnipeg, Canada
Background and Aims: In patients who receive intervention (endovascular thrombectomy [EVT] or intravenous thrombolysis [IVT]) for acute ischemic stroke (AIS), there can be intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) or contrast extravasation (CE) on 24-hour follow-up imaging. While ICH and CE look identical on single-energy CT (SECT), dual-energy CT (DECT) is supposed to be better in differentiating them. We conducted the first prospective cohort study to determine the incidence of ICH and CE and accuracy of DECT in differentiating the two.
Methods: AIS patients (anterior and posterior circulation) undergoing IVT and/or EVT were prospectively identified, recruited and underwent both SECT and DECT 24 hours post-intervention. Deferred consent was obtained. Hyperdensity on water-weighted imaging alone was ICH, hyperdensity on iodine-weighted imaging alone was CE, and hyperdensity on both images was mixed (Figure 1). Patients with hyperdensity on SECT underwent repeat imaging at 48–hour post-intervention to determine resolution of hyperdensity.

Results: Of the 200 patients recruited, 189 (Male- 107; Female- 82; mean age- 72 years) were included in the final analysis. Of these, 46 patients (24.3%) had hyperdensity on 24-hour SECT, 19 (41.3%) were classified as ICH on DECT, 13 (28.3%) as CE, and 14(30.4%) as mixed (Table 1). In patients with CE on DECT, the hyperdensity persisted on the repeat scan.
Conclusions: SECT showed hyperdensity in 24.3% of AIS patients undergoing intervention with 41% showing hemorrhage and 28% CE and the rest a mixed picture on DECT. Hyperdensity persisted in all patients with CE on 48-hour CT scan.

STUDY OF VESSEL WALL MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING IN THE DIAGNOSIS OF STROKE

Background and Aims: Vessel wall (VW) MRI has become widely available and is emerging as one of the effective methods to detect stenotic lesions and characterize pathologic features involving the VW. It helps to evaluate the disease within the vessels and beyond the lumen. Besides extra-cranial pathologies, it’s application has extended to evaluate intracranial vascular pathologies like plaques, vasculitis, moyamoya disease, aneurysm. We planned to do vessel wall MRI imaging in patients with stroke to delineate the pathology.
Methods: Patients of stroke underwent MRI vessel wall imaging (3D T2 and T1 pre and post contrast images). It was performed in 20 patients over period of one year in patients to depict non-stenotic lesions and characterise stenotic lesions.
Results: Out of 20 patients, 14 were of young stroke (<45 years) and 6 were (>45 years). Intense vessel wall enhancement was seen in 6 imaging studies s/o vasculitis. T1 hyperintense hematoma was seen in 5 patients, located in V3 vertebral and ICA petrous part. One imaging was suggestive of Moyà Moyà disease and other was showing changes of RCVS and another showed intracranial atherosclerosis. No enhancement was seen in stenosed vessel in 4 imaging studies.
Conclusions: Intracranial VW imaging has become part of state-of-the-art MR imaging protocols detecting causes of ischemic stroke. The main advantages of intracranial vessel wall (VW) imaging over lumen-based methods are detection of non-stenotic lesions and further characterization of stenotic lesions that have already been detected with common angiographic methods. This imaging technique need to be used widely.

NEUROMELIOIDOSIS CAUSING RAPIDLY PROGREASING NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS LIKE STROKE
NEUROIMAGING.S. V

Background and Aims: Neuromelioidosis can occur as a systemic manifestation in 3-5 % of cases if melioidosis. It can mimic other acute neurological disorders like stroke. We present a case if a 65 year old farmer who presented with stroke like symptoms and was later diagnosed with melioidosis. We aim to raise awareness about this potentially treatable disease.
Methods: The case sheets, Magnetic resonance imaging findings and laboratory information if the patient were acessed and reviewed.

EV310 / #2481
ASSESSMENT OF INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE VOLUMES USING THE AUTOMATED VIOLA TOOL PERFORMS SIMILARLY TO ABC/2 MEASUREMENT
NEUROIMAGING.T. Potter1, E. Aamodt2, K. Borei3, A. Bako4, A. Pan1, Q. Liu5, B. Macintosh6, F. Vahidy4
1Houston Methodist, Center For Health Data Science & Analytics, Houston, United States of America, 2Oslo University, Division Of Radiology And Nuclear Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 3Houston Methodist, Department Of Neurosurgery, Houston, United States of America, 4TIRR Memorial Hermann, Houston, United States of America, 5Oslo University Hospital, Oslo, Norway, 6University of Toronto, Medical Biophysics, Toronto, Canada
Background and Aims: Hemorrhage volume is a key prognostic characteristic for intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) patients, including use in the ICH score. Hemorrhage annotation can be time consuming, however, prompting the need for automated measurement tools. We compared estimates from the VIOLA deep learning model (developed at www.crai.no) to conventional ABC/2 measurement.
Methods: A random sample of adult (>18) ICH patients were selected from the Registry for Neurological Endpoint Assessment among patients with Ischemic and Hemorrhagic Stroke (REINAH) database. The computed tomography (CT) images used for ABC/2 measurement were retrieved, and the VIOLA deep learning tool was deployed locally for hemorrhage segmentation. ICH volumes were compared using the Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, and multivariable logistic regression models were fit to predict poor outcome (death or discharge to hospice. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) are reported.
Results: Records for 407 patients were retrieved (median age: 68 [55-77]; 42.8% female; 43.7% White, 18.7% Black, 22.4% Hispanic, 9.6% Asian, 5.7% Other/Declined), with 24.6% experiencing poor outcome. These findings highlight the need for time-sensitive, individualized treatment approaches in this population.

DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTS OF ADMISSION GLYCATED HEMOGLOBIN BY EGFR STAGES ON MORTALITY IN ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE AND DIABETES MELLITUS
OUTCOMES.J.-T. Kim1, S. Ryu2, H.-J. Bae3
1Chonnam National University Medical School, Neurology, Gwangju, Korea, Republic of, 2Cheomdan Wooam Hospital, Rehabilitation, Gwangju, Korea, Republic of, 3Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, Neurology, Seongnam, Korea, Republic of
Background and Aims: The relationship between admission HbA1c levels, eGFR stages, and early outcomes may provide key insights into the need for individualized glycemic control based on kidney function in patients with ischemic stroke(IS) and diabetes.
Methods: We analyzed data from a multicenter, nationwide, prospective stroke registry in South Korea, including patients with IS within 7 days of onset and diabetes. Admission HbA1c levels(prestroke glycemic status) were categorized as<6.0%, 6.0–7.0%, 7.0–8.0%, and ⩾8.0%. eGFR stages were classified as: stage 1(⩾90 mL/min/1.73m²), stage 2(60–89), stage 3(45–59), stage 4(15–44), and stage 5(⩽15). The primary outcome was 3-month all-cause mortality.
Results: A total of 27,496 patients(age; 69.6±11.4years, male; 60.3%) were included. The 3-month cumulative all-cause mortality rates differed significantly by admission HbA1c levels: 8.9% in HbA1c<6.0% vs. 5.3% in HbA1c⩾8.0%. In unadjusted analyses, HbA1c<6.0% was associated with higher mortality compared to HbA1c 6.0–7.0%, whereas higher HbA1c groups showed no consistent associations across eGFR stages. In adjusted analyses, the association between HbA1c<6.0% and mortality disappeared across eGFR stages. This study investigates how different living environments influence functional and psychological outcomes.
Methods: A total of 278 stroke survivors living either in their homes or nursing homes in Istanbul,Turkey were assessed. Patient outcomes were evaluated using Stroke Impact Scale, Stroke Specific Quality of Life Scale, Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia, Geriatric Depression Scale, UCLA-Loneliness Scale, and Tinetti Gait and Balance Test. Covariates included age, stroke years, education, medical history, treatments received and caregiver support.
Results: Latent Class Analysis identified two distinct patient class, as shown in figure. Class 2 demonstrated significantly better outcomes characterized by greater independence, improved quality of life, lower depression and loneliness scores, reduced kinesiophobia, lower fall risk, healthier exercise routines and sleep quality. While the overall sample included more individuals receiving home care, the class which exhibited better functional and psychological outcomes contained a higher proportion of nursing home residents.

Conclusions: These results reject the hypothesis that home living patients with family support would feel less lonely and exhibit better outcomes than those living in nursing homes. Our study highlights the importance of comprehensive, multifactorial investigations into stroke recovery trajectories and underscores the role of structured rehabilitation and medical support in promoting meaningful functional and psychological outcomes.

Madras Medical College, Neurology, Chennai, India
Background and Aims: Hyponatremia is frequently encountered in patients with acute ischemic stroke and has been postulated to influence clinical outcomes. However, its role as an independent prognostic marker remains underexplored, particularly in resource limited settings. This study aimed to evaluate its impact on functional outcomes and in hospital mortality.
Methods: This prospective analytical study was conducted over a one-year period at a tertiary care teaching hospital in South India. A total of 350 adult patients with confirmed acute ischemic stroke were enrolled and stratified into two cohorts based on the presence or absence of hyponatremia (serum sodium <135 mmol/L) at admission. Primary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and functional status at discharge, assessed using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS). Statistical analyses included chi-square tests, odds ratios (ORs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) to evaluate associations between hyponatremia and clinical outcomes. Results: Of the total cohort, 140 patients (40%) presented with hyponatremia. PROGNOSTIC VALUE OF CT PERFUSION PATTERNS IN PATIENTS WITH MINOR ISCHEMIC STROKE
OUTCOMES.F. Purroy1, L. Perez1, S. Salvany2, Y. Gallego3, A. Peguera2, C. Pereira2, G. Mauri-Capdevila3

Background and Aims: The group of patients with minor stroke (MS) has been underrepresented in reperfusion trials, yet a substantial proportion experiences poor functional outcomes at 90 days. We aimed to assess the prognostic value of multiparametric CT imaging in this population
Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study including consecutive patients with MS (NIHSS ⩽5) and a pre-stroke modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score <3, who underwent multiparametric CT within 24 hours of symptom onset between May 2021 and May 2024. Using RAPID AI software, patients were classified into three imaging patterns: no intracranial vessel occlusion (VO) and normal perfusion (VO– PF–), no VO with abnormal perfusion (VO– PF+), and VO with abnormal perfusion (VO+ PF+). Results: Among 1,933 suspected stroke cases, 468 patients were diagnosed with minor stroke, of whom 378 met the inclusion criteria. Methods: A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Nine databases were searched up to December 15, 2024. Data on study design, stroke subtype, model construction, performance (AUC, calibration, decision curve analysis), and bias (PROBAST) were extracted and analyzed.
Results: Twenty-five studies were included. Most models targeted ischemic stroke (92%) and used multivariable logistic regression (96%), with nomograms being the primary presentation (88%). Median AUC was 0.865, but calibration and external validation were underreported (44% and 32%, respectively). Only 8% of models had low risk of bias across all PROBAST domains. Common predictors included NIHSS score, age, glucose, and blood pressure.
Conclusions: Current ND prediction models show strong discriminatory performance but face challenges in calibration, external validation, and clinical applicability. Future efforts should prioritize standardized ND definitions, better reporting of calibration, and validation across diverse populations to enhance clinical utility.

Background and Aims: Cerebellar Mutism Syndrome (CMS) is a rare condition primarily described in pediatric patients post-posterior fossa surgery. Methods: We present a 30-year-old previously healthy left-handed male who developed acute dizziness, ataxia, and dysarthria after a wake-up stroke. After eight weeks of neurorehabilitation, the patient significantly improved and was discharged with a modified Rankin Scale score of 1.

Diagnosis requires high clinical suspicion supported by functional imaging. Recognition of ischemic CMS is critical to guide management and rehabilitation, even outside the typical pediatric tumor-related context.

Background and Aims: Diet plays a critical role in stroke prevention and management. The Mediterranean Diet (MedDiet) and Mediterranean-DASH Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND Diet) are recognized for their neuroprotective benefits. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the impact of adherence to these diets on stroke incidence, severity, and recovery.

Conclusions: Adherence to the MedDiet and MIND Diet significantly reduces stroke incidence, mitigates severity, and enhances recovery, particularly for ischemic stroke and cognitive outcomes.

Background and Aims: Stroke recurrence significantly increases disability and mortality in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS). The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, a simple and non-invasive surrogate marker of insulin resistance, has emerged as a potential predictor of adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular outcomes. Insulin resistance plays a pivotal role in the development of type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and stroke.
Methods: This observational study, incorporating both retrospective and prospective components, included 300 patients admitted with acute stroke between December 2023 and April 2025. The TyG index was calculated using the formula: ln [fasting glucose (mg/dL) × triglycerides (mg/dL)] / 2. Patients were categorized into three groups: Category 1 (<8.5), Category 2 (8.5–9.0), and Category 3 (>9.0). Clinical data, including NIHSS scores, comorbidities, hospital stay duration, and functional outcomes at discharge, were analyzed.

Patients in Category 3 had longer hospital stays and demonstrated poorer NIHSS score improvement and functional outcomes at discharge compared to lower TyG categories.
Conclusions: Elevated TyG index is significantly associated with increased stroke severity and poorer short-term outcomes in AIS patients. EV413 / #1497
MOTOR RECOVERY AFTER STROKE IS NOT AFFECTED BY COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENTS
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.R. Binyamin Netser1,2,3, L. Smuelof1,2, H. Idan3, T. Mizrahi3
1Ben Gurion University, Brain And Cognition, Beer sheva, Israel, 2Ben Gurion University, The Zelman Center For Brain Science Research, Beer Sheva, Israel, 3Adi Negev Nahalat Eran Rehabilitation hospital, Ofakim, Israel
Background and Aims: Rehabilitation enhances recovery through learning new motor patterns. However, motor learning relies heavily on cognitive processes, such as executive functions and memory, highlighting a potential indirect detrimental effect of cognitive impairments after brain damage on motor recovery. Despite this concern, research in this area is insufficient as most studies on motor recovery after stroke do not include cognitive assessments and often exclude patients with cognitive impairments. In this longitudinal study, we investigated the influence of cognitive impairments on motor recovery and the association between cognitive and motor recovery after stroke.
Methods: Eighty-one persons with stroke (PWS) in the subacute phase were followed from admission through 12 months post-stroke (four time points of assessment), a period during which the recovery process typically stabilizes. Patients underwent a battery of clinical assessments, evaluating their cognitive (MoCA) and motor (ARAT) function.
Results: Cognitive impairments (MoCA) one month after stroke were associated with upper extremity motor impairments (ARAT). However, motor recovery three months after stroke was not correlated with cognitive impairments one month after the stroke. Cognitive recovery was moderately correlated with motor recovery.
Conclusions: The correlation between cognitive and motor impairments and recovery suggests the existence of shared cognitive-motor neural processes. The lack of dependence between motor recovery and cognitive impairments does not support the hypothesis that cognitive resources are essential for motor recovery. This calls for refining cognitive and motor assessments before drawing further conclusions.

Immersive virtual reality (VR) facilitates guided breathing and relaxation with reduced cognitive load and environmental distractions, which may promote deeper parasympathetic responses associated with relaxation. Conclusions: Integration of immersive relaxation to reflex-inhibiting patterns appears to be promising in post-stroke spasticity management. It improves patients’ adherence to therapy by facilitating deep relaxation and reducing pain. Further studies are recommended to explore its long-term impact.

This study examines factors associated with opioid prescribing patterns following stroke.

Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 291 stroke patients admitted to our institution. Delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM). Key outcomes included change in AM-PAC scores, length of stay (LOS), discharge setting, and occupational therapy (OT) participation.
Results: 15 of the 18 patients with mobility decline were delirious (CAM+). 1University of Haifa, Department Of Physical Therapy, Faculty Of Social Welfare & Health Sciences, Haifa, Israel, 2Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Department Of Health Policy And Management, Faculty Of Health Sciences, Beer Sheva, Israel, 3Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Guilford Glazer Faculty Of Business And Management, Beer Sheva, Israel
Background and Aims: Persons living with stroke face persistent, complex health needs across multiple domains. Neurology and allied health professionals provide essential services for rehabilitation, secondary prevention, maintaining function, and promoting self-management. However, research on the long-term utilization patterns of these critical services remains limited. Accordingly, this study aimed to describe the existing evidence on long-term utilization of stroke-related healthcare services and utilization rates.
Methods: A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published between 2010 and 2023. Inclusion criteria encompassed research reporting utilization of stroke-related medical or rehabilitative services by community-dwelling persons living with stroke in the chronic phase. Data on study characteristics, methodological approaches, and utilization outcomes were collected.
Results: Fourteen studies met inclusion criteria, encompassing 204,879 participants in 12 countries. Studies varied by data sources and measurement formats. A REVIEW OF CLINICAL STUDIES IN KOREA ON KOREAN MEDICINE TREATMENT FOR POST-STROKE SPASTICITY AND SUGGESTIONS FOR THE SELECTION OF EVALUATION TOOLS

Kyung Hee University, Clinical Korean Medicine, Seoul, Korea, Republic of
Background and Aims: Post-stroke spasticity is a common complication that significantly impairs functional recovery and quality of life. This study aims to critically review domestic Korean research trends on Korean medicine treatments for post-stroke spasticity and to suggest appropriate outcome measures for clinical and research applications.
Methods: A comprehensive search was conducted across six major Korean academic databases without year limitations, identifying studies involving Korean medicine interventions for spasticity. Inclusion criteria allowed studies regardless of design type, and treatment modalities were categorized and analyzed along with the outcome assessment tools employed.
Results: Eighteen studies were included. Conclusions: Korean medicine interventions such as electroacupuncture may be beneficial for post-stroke spasticity. However, there is a need to update the evaluation framework, with MAS replaced or supplemented by MTS and NRS-S for enhanced objectivity and patient-centered assessment. Jeju National University Hospital, Jeju National University School of Medicine, Department Of Rehabilitation Medicine, JEJU-SI, Korea, Republic of
Background and Aims: The phase angle(PhA) derived from bioelectrical impedance analysis(BIA) has emerged as an important prognostic tool in clinical practice. The aim of this study was to evaluate the associations between PhA and physical function, including sarcopenia and arterial stiffness, in patients with stroke.
Methods: We conducted a single-center, retrospective, observational study. We evaluated 57 stroke patients who were admitted to the Neuro Vascular Center of this hospital. Upon transfer to the rehabilitation department, we conducted several assessments, including Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis(BIA), brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity(baPWV), ankle-brachial index(ABI), and various physical function tests. Functional assessment included the Korean version of the Mini-Mental State Examination(K-MMSE), the modified Rankin Scale(mRS), the Functional Ambulatory Category(FAC), the Berg Balance Scale (BBS), the Timed Up and Go(TUG) test, the 10-Meter Walk Test(10MWT), the Korean version of the Modified Barthel Index(K-MBI), and the Manual Functional Test(MFT). These assessments were performed at the time of transfer to the rehabilitation department and again at discharge.
Results: In males, age, BMI, SMI, ECW ratio, mRS, FAC, BBS, K-MBI, MFT on the intact side, grip strength on the intact side, and baPWV showed significant correlations with phase angle. In females, weight, BMI, SMI, ECW ratio, K-MMSE, BBS, TUG test, MFT on the intact side, MFT on the hemiplegic side, grip strength on the intact side, and baPWV were significantly correlated with phase angle.
Conclusions: The findings of this study indicate that the BIA-derived phase angle is positively associated with physical function, sarcopenia, and arterial stiffness in stroke patients.

TO EXPLORE THE KNOWLEDGE, ATTITUDE AND PRACTICE (KAP) OF THE MULTI-DISCIPLINARY TEAM (MDT) IN SUPPORTING THE WELL-BEING OF INPATIENTS WITH POST STROKE DYSPHAGIA (PSD)
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.N. Lennard, A. Seckam
Cardiff Metropolitan University, School Of Sport And Health Sciences, Cardiff, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Introduction Dysphagia or swallowing difficulties are common following stroke. There are limited studies exploring MDT members who support people with PSD in particular, their KAP regarding the impact of PSD towards well-being and quality of life (QoL).
Methods: A survey design with the use of a questionnaire was disseminated to MDT members working in stroke settings across Wales. The data was analysed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), content analysis and thematic analysis.
Results: Forty-nine (n=49) stroke specific MDT staff participated in this study. Good internal consistency was found of the questionnaire dataset was found (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.87). Overall, the cohort demonstrated that they have good knowledge of PSD and had a positive attitude towards working with people who have PSD. It was also demonstrated that the MDT were able to support patient well-being. The amount of working experience had a statistically significant impact on whether staff felt anxious supporting people with PSD to eat and drink (x2(3, N=49) = p0.04). Themes regarding best practice and barriers to effective care of people with PSD have been identified; including: ‘Resources’, ‘MDT knowledge and experience’, and ‘Patient choice and environment’.
Conclusions: Conclusion The results obtained from this cohort has provided insights into the KAP of the MDT in supporting the well-being of inpatients with PSD. This survey provides an underpinning for the further development and exploration of this topic. There is also scope to develop staff education to target this area and further research is warranted.

SELF-REPORTED AND OBJECTIVE SLEEP MEASURES: THEIR ROLE IN POST-STROKE FATIGUE AMONG ACUTE STROKE PATIENTS- (NORFAST)
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.D. Simpson1, C. Gay2,3, S. Berg4, C. English5, H. Ihle-Hansen6,7, G. Helland8,9, P. Larsson10,11, I. Johansen12, J. Stubberud3,13, B. Øverland4, A. Lerdal3,11
1University of Newcastle, College Of Health, Medicine And Wellbeing, Callaghan, Australia, 2University of Califorina San Francisco, School Of Nursing, San Francisco, United States of America, 3Lovisenberg Diaconal Hospital, Research Department, Oslo, Norway, 4Lovisenberg Diaconal Hospital, Department Of Sleep Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 5Hunter Medical Research Institute, Newcastle, Australia, 6Oslo University Hospital, Department Of Acute Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 7University of Oslo, Center For Medical Ethics, Oslo, Norway, 8Oslo University Hospital, Department Of Neurology, Oslo, Norway, 9Vestre Viken Hospital Trust, Department Of Medical Research, Drammen, Norway, 10Lovisenberg Diaconal Hospital, Surgical Department, Oslo, Norway, 11University of Oslo, Department Of Public Health Science, Institute Of Health And Society, Faculty Of Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 12VID Specialized University, Institute Of Nursing, Faculty Of Health Science, Oslo, Norway, 13University of Oslo, Institute Of Psychology, Oslo, Norway
Background and Aims: Post-stroke fatigue in the acute phase often impacts rehabilitation, daily activities, and overall quality of life. The relationship between sleep and fatigue remains unclear. This study aimed to: a) assess fatigue and sleep through both self-reported and objective measures, b) describe sleep apnea, and c) explore the associations between sleep measures and post-stroke fatigue during the acute phase.
Methods: A cross-sectional study examining Norwegian adults within 14 days of first ischemic stroke. Fatigue was assessed with the Fatigue Severity Scale. Self-reported sleep factors (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index [PSQI], Epworth Sleepiness Scale) and objective WatchPAT measures (apnoea-hypopnea, sleep time, efficiency, REM and deep sleep) served as exposure variables. Multivariable regression models, adjusted for age, sex, modified Rankin Scale, and depression and anxiety symptoms, were used to examine associations between sleep and fatigue.
Results: Participants (n=107, mean age 65 (SD 14) years, n=65(61%) male) had a mean NIHSS score of 2.5 [SD 3.3], Fatigue Severity Scale score of 3.11 [SD 1.82], and n=71 (66%) had disturbed sleep (PSQI⩾5). Mean total sleep time (n=81) was 7.04 [SD 1.46] hours and 54 (71%) had sleep apnoea. In the final model, only poor self-reported sleep quality (b=0.45, p=0.010) was associated with post-stroke fatigue; no other sleep factors, including sleep apnoea, were associated.
Conclusions: During the acute stroke phase, more than half of the participants experienced post-stroke fatigue and sleep disturbances, with two-thirds having sleep apnea. Only sleep quality was associated with fatigue. Interventions to improve sleep quality during initial hospitalization may help alleviate post-stroke fatigue.

ASSESSMENT OF THE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL CONSISTENCY OF BIOMETRICS DEVICES IN TERMS OF HAND GRIP AND FINGER PINCH STRENGTH IN PEOPLE AFTER STROKE
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.J. Leszczak, B. Pniak, J. Baran, A. Guzik
University of Rzeszow, Faculty Of Health Sciences And Psychology, Collegium Medicum, Rzeszów, Poland
Background and Aims: The aim of the study was to assess the consistency of an internal and external Biometrics device with regard to hand grip and finger pinch strength in people in the late period after stroke.
Methods: The study was conducted among 100 people in the late period after a stroke. Two investigators performed hand grip and pinch strength measurements using the Biometrics E-link EP9 assessment system. The subjects were examined twice within two weeks, under the same conditions.
Results: After conducting the examinations, high consistency of measurements was found both between the investigators and between the examinations using a hand grip dynamometer and a Pinchmeter. For all measurements, high values of Pearson correlation coefficient close to 1, interclass correlation coefficient (ICC) > 0.9 and Cronbach’s alpha index > 0.9 were shown.
Conclusions: The study showed that hand grip and pinch strength assessment performed using the Biometrics E-link EP9 assessment system show high internal and external consistency.
The Biometrics E-link EP9 can be recommended for daily clinical practice among people in the late period after stroke.

A REVIEW OF REHABILITATION METHODS AIMED AT IMPROVING LOWER LIMB FUNCTION IN PATIENTS IN THE ACUTE PHASE OF STROKE
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.J. Leszczak1, K. Laskowska2
1University of Rzeszow, Faculty Of Health Sciences And Psychology, Collegium Medicum, Rzeszów, Poland, 2University of Rzeszów, Student Scientific Circle „rehavita” Faculty Of Health Sciences And Psychology, Collegium Medicum, Rzeszów, Poland
Background and Aims: Stroke remains the third leading cause of death and the main cause of adult disability in Europe. Approximately 610,000 strokes occur annually in the EU, with projections reaching 820,000 by 2035 due to population aging. In Poland, around 90,000 cases are reported each year, 30% of which involve individuals under 65. Despite progress in acute care, the 30-day mortality rate in Poland (13%) remains above the EU average (7.7%). Early and intensive rehabilitation is key to recovery, with nearly half of patients having the potential to regain function. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of lower limb rehabilitation in the acute phase of stroke.
Methods: The review followed PRISMA guidelines. A database search (PUBMED, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect) conducted in April 2025 identified randomized controlled trials assessing the impact of rehabilitation on lower limb function in acute stroke patients. Fifteen articles meeting inclusion criteria were analyzed.
Results: A total of 1,496 patients were included. Effective interventions included bilateral transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, the REX rehabilitation exoskeleton, constraint-induced movement therapy, plyometric exercises, robot-assisted gait training, botulinum toxin injections, acupuncture, and recumbent cycle ergometer training. These methods improved lower limb function, muscle strength, joint mobility, and quality of life.
Conclusions: Despite positive outcomes, the limited number of studies highlights the need for further randomized controlled trials to draw more comprehensive conclusions regarding the effectiveness of early lower limb rehabilitation after stroke.

REVIEW OF THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS FOR UPPER LIMB REHABILITATION AFTER STROKE IN PATIENTS IN THE ACUTE PHASE
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.J. Leszczak1, R. Nowak2
1University of Rzeszow, Faculty Of Health Sciences And Psychology, Collegium Medicum, Rzeszów, Poland, 2University of Rzeszów, Student Scientific Circle „rehavita” Faculty Of Health Sciences And Psychology, Collegium Medicum, Rzeszów, Poland
Background and Aims: Stroke is a prevalent neurological condition with high disability and mortality rates. Each year, around 1.1 million people in Europe suffer strokes, a figure projected to rise to 1.5 million by 2025, increasing demand for neurological rehabilitation. Hemiplegia, a common outcome, leads to motor limitations affecting daily life. Despite rehabilitation efforts, 33%-66% of patients fail to recover upper limb function within six months post-stroke. This review aims to assess the effectiveness of upper limb rehabilitation during the acute phase.
Methods: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. Information was obtained in March 2025 by searching the PUBMED, Google Scholar and SinceDirect database for randomized controlled trials assessing the efficacy of rehabilitation in restoring upper limb function after acute stroke.
Results: Fifteen articles meeting the inclusion criteria were incorporated into this systematic review. Most participants experienced ischaemic stroke in the acute phase. Results showed that various types of physiotherapy (like robot-assisted therapy, rehabilitation with VR, transcranial direct current stimulation and others) can significantly improve the outcomes of the rehabilitation.
Conclusions: Results point out that training based on innovative methods of physiotherapy with conventional physiotherapy improve upper limb activity to patients in acute phase, what is important in physiotherapy later. Nevertheless, the limited number of articles included in this review highlights the need for additional randomized controlled trials on this topic to enable the formulation of more comprehensive conclusions.

NEUROPHYSIOLOGICAL EFFECTS OF ONABOTULINUMTOXINA INJECTION IN PATIENTS WITH POST-STROKE SPASTICITY
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.M.F. Levin1,2, J. Khayat1,2, A. Feldman2,3, T. Wein4
1McGill University, School Of Physical And Occupational Therapy, Montreal, Canada, 2Centre for Interdisciplinary Research in Rehabilitation of Greater Montreal (CRIR), Montreal, Canada, 3University of Montreal, Department Of Neuroscience, Montreal, Canada, 4McGill University, Neurology, Montreal, Canada
Background and Aims: Spasticity is a major barrier to stroke recovery. Physical and pharmacological therapy for spasticity focuses on relieving discomfort and increasing functional capacity. Physical treatments have only short-term effects. No medication currently available completely alleviates spasticity and many have undesirable side effects, such as fatigue and drowsiness. A notable exception is OnabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA), approved for spasticity treatment. Despite its prevalence, efficacy studies are marred by measures with insufficient sensitivity for evaluating changes in both the clinical and reflex aspects of spasticity. Aim: To characterize neurophysiological properties of the stretch reflex and clinical changes in order to determine the effectiveness and time-course of onabotA treatment.
Methods: Stretch reflex excitability is measured by the angle of onset of the tonic stretch reflex threshold (TSRT) and the velocity-sensitivity of the threshold. Patients with stroke (0-12 mo) with upper or lower limb moderate-to-severe spasticity are recruited to a multiple baseline single-subject AB design study. Following baseline assessment (A), onabotA is injected in the target muscle(s) and assessments are done weekly/bi-weekly until 12 weeks post-injection (B) plus 1-month follow-up. Assessments include TSRT angle, velocity-sensitivity of the stretch response, sensation, PROM, AROM, strength, resistance to passive stretch, motor impairment level (Fugl-Meyer scale), ultrasound imaging and MRI.
Results: Initial results in 7 patients (5 upper limb, 2 lower limb) suggest that following onabotA injection, TSRT angle and velocity-sensitivity of the stretch reflex improve along with improvements in clinical impairment in most patients.
Conclusions: Recruitment will continue until a final cohort of 44 patients is achieved.

ROCK1-MEDIATED DYSFUNCTION OF LYSOSOMAL ACIDIFICATION IN REGULATING SYNAPTIC PLASTICITY OF POST STROKE COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.H. Li1, Y.-B. Hu2, G. Li1
1Shanghai East Hospital, School of Medicine, Tongji University, Department Of Neurology, Shanghai, China, 2Shanghai Changhai Hospital, Shanghai, China
Background and Aims: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI), a highly disabling complication following stroke, is mechanistically linked to synaptic plasticity deficits mediated by impaired lysosomal acidification. This study investigates the molecular mechanisms by which Rho kinase ROCK1 regulates lysosomal function.
Methods: Employed dMCAO mouse models and oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R)-induced neuronal injury models, and integrated multi-omics analyses, molecular biology, behavioral evaluations systematically elucidate the pivotal role of ROCK1 in PSCI pathogenesis.
Results: Bioinformatics and clinical data analyses reveal upregulated ROCK1 expression in both brain tissues and peripheral blood of PSCI patients, showing negative correlations with MMSE and MoCA scores. Animal experiments demonstrate elevated hippocampal ROCK1 levels at 8 weeks post-modeling, accompanied by reduced dendritic spine density. Targeted ROCK1 inhibition restores lysosomal acidification, enhances postsynaptic density thickness and ameliorates cognitive deficits as evidenced by elevated novel object recognition indices and shortened escape latency in the Morris water maze test.
Conclusions: This study pioneers in elucidating the ROCK1 as a critical regulator of synaptic remodeling, offering novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets for PSCI prevention and treatment.
EV463 / #862
THE CLEARANCE OF NEUTROPHIL EXTRACELLULAR TRAPS BY CONSTRAINT-INDUCED MOVEMENT THERAPY DEPENDS ON MICROGLIA
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.C. Li, Y. Hua, M. Liu, J. Hu, Y. Bai
Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai, China
Background and Aims: Our previous studies have demonstrated that constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) alleviates motor impairment by inhibiting the accumulation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in ischemic cortex. The purpose of this study is to determine whether the clearance effect of CIMT on NETs is related to microglia and its specific mechanism.
Methods: Administration of the Colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor inhibitor PLX3397 and intraperitoneal injection of minocycline were used to deplete and inactivate microglia, respectively. Furthermore, microglia after CIMT intervention were sorted out by Magnet-activated cell sorting for transcriptome sequencing, GO and KEGG enrichment analysis. GSEA was used to further cluster the expression of genes related to microglia phagocytosis pathway.
Results: Immunofluorescence results showed that iba1+ microglia branched around CitH3 protein in ischemic cortex, while CIMT increased CD68+ lysosome expression in microglia. After microglia depletion with PLX3397 and functional inhibition of microglia with minocycline, CIMT treatment failed to reduce NETs indexes such as CitH3, MPO and NE while CIMT resumed its inhibitory effect on NETs after microglia replantation. Intriguingly, CIMT increased the proportion of CD86+ pro-inflammatory microglia after the injection of minocycline. The results of RNA-seq indicated that CIMT significantly up-regulated the phagocytic process of microglia and increased IL-33/ST2 expression in ischemic cortex.
Conclusions: CIMT mediates the phagocytosis of NETs by microglia in ischemic cortex and is beneficial to maintain the balance of pro-inflammatory/anti-inflammatory microglia. The synaptic budding is at least partially attributed to the spatial location provided by microglial phagocytosis of NETs. IL-33/ST2 may be the target mediating this phagocytosis.

UNDERSTANDING DIGITAL HEALTH LITERACY AMONG STROKE SURVIVORS: A CLUSTER ANALYSIS APPROACH (NORFAST)
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.A.-M. Linnestad1, I. Skogestad2, C. Gay3, C. Borge1, J. Stubberud4, B. Indredavik5, A. Lerdal1
1University of Oslo, Department Of Public Health Science, Institute Of Health And Society, Faculty Of Medicine, Oslo, Norway, 2VID Specialized University, Institute Of Nursing, Faculty Of Health Science, Oslo, Norway, 3School of Nursing, University of California San Francisco, CA, United States of America, 4University of Oslo, Department Of Psychology, Oslo, Norway, 5University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Department Of Neuroscience (inm), Torgarden, Trondheim, Norway
Background and Aims: Digital health technologies are increasingly used to improve stroke prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation. However, stroke survivors vary in their confidence and skills in using these tools, with differences in digital health literacy (DHL) potentially limiting effective use. Knowledge about DHL profiles and their associated factors is needed to tailor interventions. Aim:
This study aims to identify distinct DHL profiles among stroke survivors and examine differences in sociodemographic and clinical characteristics across these groups.
Methods:
A cross-sectional study recruited 177 patients with first-ever stroke (2021–2022) from the Norwegian Stroke Registry. DHL was assessed using the 7-domain eHealth Literacy Questionnaire (eHLQ). Cluster analysis identified DHL profiles, and multinomial regression evaluated associations with demographic and clinical variables, adjusting for relevant covariates.
Results: Three DHL clusters were identified: 1) Novices (26%), 2) Cautious users (57%), and 3) Navigators (17%). Novices reported severe DHL limitations, Cautious users exhibited intermediate DHL levels, and Navigators demonstrated high DHL levels. In adjusted analyses with Cautious users as the reference group, participants ⩾67 years had a five-fold higher risk of being a Novice, and those with lower education or lower cognitive functioning were also at higher risk of being a Novice. Additionally, those living alone were less likely to be a Navigator than a Cautious user.
Conclusions:
This study highlights diverse DHL profiles among stroke survivors, underscoring the need for personalized digital health services and targeted interventions to improve DHL. Enhancing DHL is essential for promoting health equity and ensuring effective use of digital health solutions.

Conclusions: We will reflect on the lessons learned—from planning and pacing sessions to ensuring participants are supported after sessions end. Along with what has worked well, we’re still learning in our commitment to accessible and inclusive co-production.

1FCS Blanquerna URL, Barcelona, Spain, 2PPSL, Barcelona, Spain
Background and Aims: Recovery of function in people with central nervous system (CNS) injury after stroke is very much like a relearning process that takes advantage of preserved sensorimotor circuits. Relearning can be optimised by providing appropriate proprioceptive (or deep sensory) information to the spinal cord with the aim of maximally engaging the preserved neural circuits. The development of the SURA electrodevice offers this sensitive input mechanism The study evaluates the impact of the SURA device on the functional recovery of stroke (CVA) patients, focusing on dynamic balance.
Methods: It is a randomized controlled clinical trial with 30 participants, dividing the subjects into an intervention group with the device activated and a control group without activation. The intervention included motor point stimulation of the gastrocnemius, soleus, and peroneal muscles, combined with standard rehabilitation sessions.
Results: Preliminary results showed significant improvements in balance (measured by the Berg scale), gait speed (10-meter walk test), and muscle strength, particularly in hip and ankle flexion and extension. Additionally, the intervention group demonstrated superior motor control, as reflected in electromyography, with more stable and synchronized muscle activation patterns, approaching values seen in healthy subjects. Improvements in joint range of motion in the hip and ankle were also observed, suggesting better control in the gait cycle.
Conclusions: The conclusions indicate that the SURA device could facilitate neuroplastic reorganization in stroke patients by providing a peripheral proprioceptive stimulus that influences the planning and execution of motor commands. Its accessible and non-invasive nature positions it as a promising tool for community-based rehabilitation.

Background and Aims: Sleep related breathing disorders (SRBD) represent a major public health issue, particularly in relation to strokes. Strokes are both a risk factor for SRBD and conversely, SRBD can increase the risk of stroke. There is limited data available on SRBD following a stroke in sub-Saharan Africa.
The aim of this study was to evaluate SRBD in patients who had suffered a stroke at the Douala General Hospital (DGH).
Methods: This was a cross-sectional analytical study conducted on patients followed in neurology department after a stroke confirmed by brain imaging. Patients with chronic respiratory diseases, cerebral venous thrombosis, or subarachnoid haemorrhage were excluded. SRBD assessment was carried out via nocturnal oximetric recording. Factors associated with SRBD were identified through logistic regression.
Results: Among the 110 patients included, 71.8% suffered from SRBD, with 58.2% having mild SRBD, 29.1% moderate, and 12.7% severe. Independent predictive factors for SRBD were android obesity (PR = 4.95), a high Mallampati score (PR = 6.69), and a high-risk Stopbang questionnaire (PR = 3.88).
Conclusions: Three out of four patients with stroke present SRBD. Screening and management of obesity and oropharyngeal obstructions could reduce their frequency.

However, the successful implementation of HIE in post-stroke rehabilitation depends on various factors. This study examines the perceived facilitators and barriers to HIE post-stroke from both patients and clinicians, using a mixed-methods approach that combines a questionnaire and exploratory qualitative interviews.
Methods: A total of 60 clinicians and stroke survivors who had implemented or participated in HIE post stroke participated in the questionnaire. Of these, 15 clinicians and 15 patients were selected for in-depth interviews. Quantitative data from the questionnaire were consolidated, while qualitative data from the interviews were recorded, transcribed, coded, and thematically analyzed.

● Does HIE increase the risk of adverse events?
