EXPLORING OPPORTUNITIES FOR FAMILY INVOLVEMENT IN STROKE REHABILITATION: INSIGHTS FROM STROKE SURVIVORS AND FAMILY MEMBERS
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.O. Manning1,2, A. Wu1, Z. Butt1, D. Kessler1,2
1Queen’s University, School Of Rehabilitation Therapy, Kingston, Canada, 2Providence Care Hospital, Kingston, Canada
Background and Aims: The provision of therapy across the stroke continuum of care is dependent on therapist capacity, which can limit opportunities for meaningful engagement in recovery-enhancing activities and lead to prolonged periods of sedentary time. Involving families in rehabilitation may help address these gaps, support continuity of care, and improve recovery. However, patient and family preferences, and facilitators and barriers to family participation are poorly understood. This study aimed to explore how families can be more meaningfully involved in stroke rehabilitation across settings.
Methods: Using a qualitative interpretive descriptive approach, semi structured interviews were conducted with stroke survivors and family members. To date, 15 interviews have been completed (8 stroke survivors, 7 family members). Data are being analyzed inductively to identify key themes and practical insights.
Results: Preliminary findings highlight that family involvement in rehabilitation is highly individualized and influenced by factors such as patient motivation, family readiness, and capacity. Participants identified the value of families for emotional support and informal monitoring of rehabilitation. Key supports included clear communication from healthcare providers, practical resources (e.g., videos, checklists), and training on how to safely assist. Involvement was seen as especially helpful during care transitions and for promoting reintegration through shared meaningful activities. Challenges included concerns about burden and inclusion in acute care. Research is ongoing; Final themes will be presented.
Conclusions: Families can play a critical role in stroke rehabilitation when supported and equipped to do so. Findings will inform development of an approach to include families in therapy.
EV472 / #1471
EFFECTS OF A TASK-SPECIFIC AND GOAL-ORIENTED REHABILITATION PORGRAM FOR ENHANCING UPPER LIMB MOTOR FUNCTION IN LATE CHRONIC STROKE
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.G. Manrique Gutierrez1,2, J. Quinzaños Fresnedo1, A. Ramirez Nava1, S. Blancas Silva1
1Instituto Nacional de Rehabilitación “Luis Guillermo Ibarra Ibarra”, Neurological Rehabilitation Division, Mexico City, Mexico, 2Faculty of Medicine, National Autonomous University of Mexico, Program Of Combined Studies In Medicine (pecem), Mexico City, Mexico
Background and Aims: Stroke remains one of the most devastating diseases, with upper limb impairment significantly affecting survivors’ quality of life. Substantial motor recovery usually occurs within the first 3–6 months post-stroke, and many individuals continue to experience persistent upper limb dysfunction afterwards. The aim of this study was to determine whether motor and functional changes of the upper limb are present after a conventional rehabilitation program.
Methods: Late chronic stroke patients underwent 20 sessions of conventional, task-specific and goal-oriented physical therapy focused on the affected upper extremity. Motor function and independence were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment: Upper Extremity (FMA-UE), Action Research Arm Test (ARAT), Functional Independence Measure (FIM), and Motor Activity Log (MAL-30). Neuroplasticity was evaluated using quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG), analyzing changes in the Delta-Theta-Alpha-Beta (DTAB) ratio and Paired-Derived Brain Symmetry Index (pdBSI).
Results: Six participants (mean age: 44.2 years; mean time since stroke onset: 8.4 years) showed statistically significant improvements across all measures: FMA-UE (∆+5.33, p=0.019), ARAT (∆+3.00, p=0.041), FIM (∆+5.00, p=0.017), MAL-30 Quantity (∆+27.17, p=0.006), and MAL-30 Quality (∆+15.50, p=0.010). Higher educational attainment correlated strongly with greater motor gains (Kendall’s τ=0.86, p=0.024). qEEG data showed a reduction in DTAB ratio (6.30 to 4.82) and pdBSI (0.29 to 0.26), indicating favorable neuroplastic changes.
Conclusions: Findings support the potential for meaningful motor recovery and increased functional independence in late chronic stroke through conventional, task-specific and goal-oriented physical therapy. Improvements were corroborated by both behavioral assessments and qEEG biomarkers, reinforcing the concept of long-term neuroplasticity.
EV473 / #1609
EFFECT OF GOAL-DIRECTED CARE BUNDLE ON HEMATOMA CHANGE IN ACUTE INTRACEREBRAL HAEMORRHAGE: SUBSTUDY OF INTERACT3 TRIAL
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.Y. Mao
Institute of Science and Technology for Brain-inspired Intelligence, Fudan Uniersity, Shanghai, China
Background and Aims: The INTERACT3 confirmed the positive effect of early implementation of an intensive care bundle in patients with acute intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). The association between the care bundle and the clinical benefit of hematoma improvement remains unclear. The computed tomography (CT) imaging substudy of the INTERACT3 study was designed to evaluate the hematoma change and clinical significance when comparing the care bundle with usual care.
Methods: Data were derived from the INTERACT3 study, including patients with baseline, 24-hour, and 7-day computed tomography (CT)scans. The care bundle included early intensive reduction of systolic blood pressure, control of blood glucose, body temperature and international normalized ratio. The primary endpoint was 24-hour relative hematoma change.
Results: A total of 1440 patients (mean age 61.7 ± 12.6 years; 66.4% of male, 85.3% of Asian) were included, among which 988 patients had available baseline and 24-hour CT scan data. The median hematoma volumes at baseline, 24-hour, and 7-day were 12.4 [interquartile range (IQR) 5.8 - 25.3] mL, 11.8 (IQR 5.1 - 21.6) mL, and 8.9 (IQR 3.6 - 17.8) mL, respectively. There was no significant difference in the relative hematoma change at 24-hour between the two groups (adjusted odds ratio: 1.01; 95% confidence interval: 0.73, 1.40, p = 0.954). The results of sensitivity and subgroup analyses were consistent.
Conclusions: Compared with usual care, the implementation of the care bundle in acute ICH patients was not associated with changes in hematoma growth at 24-hour or 7-day.
EV474 / #1197
FUNCTIONAL ELECTRICAL STIMULATION (FES) OF THE LOWER LIMBS IMPROVES WALKING ABILITY IN STROKE PATIENTS WITH HEMIPLEGIA DURING THE EARLY STAGES OF INDEPENDENT WALKING
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.S. Matsumoto1, M. Shimodozono2
1Ibaraki Prefectural University of Health Sciences, Center For Medical Science, Ami-Cho, Japan, 2Kagoshima University, Department Of Rehabilitation And Physical Medicine, Kagoshima City, Japan
Background and Aims: We evaluated whether the functional electrical stimulation (FES) of the lower limbs could effectively improve walking ability and lower extremity function in post-stroke patients with foot drop (RALLY Study, Matsumoto, et. al. JCM 2023). We further stratified and reanalyzed the RALLY Study data according to walking function (Functional Ambulation Category, FAC).
Methods: Patients aged 20–85 years with an initial stroke in ⩽6 months and a functional ambulation classification score of 3 or 4 were eligible. Patients were randomly allocated to FES or control group in a 1:1 ratio. A 40-min training program using FES was additionally performed by the FES group five times per week for 8 weeks. The control group received the 40-min training program without FES. We stratified the RALLY Study data based on FAC categories 3 and 4 at baseline and compared changes in 6-minute walk distance (6MWT), 10-meter walk speed (10mWT), and Timed Up and Go (TUG) between the lower limb FES group and the control group at baseline and at follow-up, all measured barefoot.
Results: In FAC 3, statistically significant improvements were observed in the lower limb FES group compared to the control group in the 6MWT and 10mWT, and a trend toward improvement was observed in comfortable walking in the TUG. On the other hand, in FAC 4, no statistically significant improvements were observed in any of the evaluation items.
Conclusions: In the early stages of independent walking (supervised walking level) during the stroke recovery process, frequent use of FES was shown to improve walking ability.
EV475 / #1190
EXPERIENCE WITH THE USE OF BRAIN-MACHINE INTERFACE FOR HAND AND FINGER DYSFUNCTION AFTER STROKE: A CASE REPORT
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.S. Matsumoto1, Y. Shuto2, T. Kasuga2, Y. Narumoto2, N. Ishibashi2
1Ibaraki Prefectural University of Health Sciences, Center For Medical Science, Ami-Cho, Japan, 2Shinyachiyo Hospital, Department Of Rehabilitation, Yaachiyo City, Japan
Background and Aims: Stroke is a leading cause of disability in adults in many countries. Hemiparesis of the upper extremity is a common problem in stroke patients. More than two-thirds of people have UE paresis in the acute phase which persists in half of the population affected by this disease to 6 months after stroke. Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) establish direct communication channels between users and computers, circumventing conventional neural pathways between the brain and muscles. BMI is a term encompassing technologies that integrate neuroscience and artificial intelligence, and it is expected to expand the possibilities of rehabilitation for patients with severe hemiplegia following stroke.
Methods: The patient was a 49-year-old woman who underwent BMI treatment two months after the onset of cerebral hemorrhage. In addition to standard rehabilitation treatment during hospitalization, she underwent a total of 10 BMI interventions.
Results: In a comparison before and after BMI intervention, all of the following showed remarkable improvement: Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper extremity (FMA-UE) and active range of motion (A-ROM), which are used to evaluate hemiplegia; The action research arm test (ARAT), which is used to evaluate object manipulation tasks; modified Ashworth scale (MAS), which is used to evaluate muscle tone; and the modified Barthel index (MBI), which is used to evaluate activities of daily living (ADL).
Conclusions: BMI has been shown to significantly improve upper extremity function and ADL in patients with subacute stroke compared to conventional rehabilitation therapy alone. The combination of BMI with other treatments that is most effective remains under discussion, and further clinical studies are needed.
EV476 / #2390
EVALUATING A COST-EFFECTIVE WIRELESS, WEARABLE BRAIN-COMPUTER INTERFACE FOR GUIDED MOTOR IMAGERY
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.C. Mccarney, K. Ruddy, O. Akhmetova, E. Mcnickle
Queen’s University Belfast, School Of Psychology, Belfast, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Although Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) show promise for stroke motor rehabilitation, clinical use remains limited. Enabling unsupervised home-based BCI training may improve adoption. Previously, we showed healthy participants could control a wireless wearable BCI using motor imagery (Simon et al., 2022). In this study, we sought to replicate the former findings using a more affordable, EEG hardware that would allow scalability of the approach for neurorehabilitation.
Methods: Nineteen participants trained for six days using a 14 channel EMOTIV EPOC wearable EEG cap with saline-soaked sponge electrodes. The BCI used common spatial patterns and linear discriminant analysis to classify mental states and provide real-time feedback. The primary outcome was classification accuracy of mental state during BCI training. Participants trained with real-time feedback of EEG activity for 4 blocks, imagining hand movement in a task that we have previously shown modulates excitability of stroke-affected limbs. Sixteen of the 19 participants completed the experiment, attending all 6 sessions. A linear mixed effects model was employed to establish whether classification accuracies improved over time, indicated by a positive slope when classification accuracy is plotted as a function of training block number.
Results: There was no significant effect of ‘training block number’ (slope=-0.015156, Confidence Interval -0.049603 0.019291, p=0.38753). Since the confidence interval does include 0, the slope of the learning curve is not significant.
Conclusions: Results suggest that the choice of EEG hardware for wireless, wearable BCI impacts outcomes considerably, and suggests that further testing of alternative cost-effective EEG systems is warranted to ensure future scalability of the approach.
EV477 / #2400
TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION NEUROFEEDBACK – A MULTIMODAL, MULTIPHASE APPROACH TO STROKE REHABILITATION USING EEG BCI
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.E. Mcnickle1, C. Simon2, K. Ruddy1
1Queen’s University Belfast, School Of Psychology, Belfast, United Kingdom, 2Trinity College Dublin, Institute Of Neuroscience, Dublin, Ireland
Background and Aims: Motor Imagery (MI)-based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) show promise for early motor rehabilitation post-stroke, a phase marked by both severe impairment and heightened neuroplasticity. However, current Electroencephalography (EEG)-based BCIs require extensive training. This study explores whether a two-phase, multimodal approach using Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation-derived Neurofeedback (TMS-NF) can accelerate BCI learning.
Methods: In a proof-of-concept study, 34 healthy young adults were divided into two groups. In phase one, 17 participants received two sessions of MI training with TMS-NF targeting muscle responses. In phase two, these participants underwent three sessions of EEG-BCI training. A control group (N=17) received five sessions of EEG-BCI training only. Classification accuracy in the EEG-BCI task was compared between groups.
Results: Participants trained with TMS-NF rapidly learned to modulate motor-evoked potential amplitudes using MI. Subsequently, they achieved higher classification accuracy and faster control of the EEG-BCI compared to the control group.
Conclusions: Pre-training with TMS-NF may foster effective MI strategies that transfer efficiently to EEG-BCI use, enabling quicker and more accurate control. This two-phase approach—beginning with TMS-NF during the acute post-stroke period and followed by home-based EEG-BCI—could enhance the feasibility and effectiveness of early rehabilitation using portable, wireless technologies.
EV478 / #1523
DETERMINING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF THE NIGERIAN LIFE AFTER STROKE CENTRE (LASC) PROGRAM
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.R. Melifonwu1, I. Onwuekwe2, O. Osi-Ogbu3, A. Ojimba4, J. Bosch5
1Stroke Action Nigeria, Life After Stroke Centre, Onitsha, Nigeria, 2University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital, Neurology, STATE, Nigeria, 3National Hospital, Internal Medicine, FCT, Nigeria, 4Federal Medical Center, Asaba, Centre For Communicable Disease Control And Research, Asaba, Nigeria, 5McMaster University, Hamilton, Canada
Background and Aims: In Nigeria, stroke affects 1.14 per 1000 people with 40% fatality rate within 30-days. Data on its impact is limited. Post stroke rehabilitation are scarce in hospital or community settings (Roushdy et al., 2022). A non-governmental organization in Onitsha, Anambra State, established a community-based Life After Stroke Centre (LASC) offering post-stroke rehabilitation to stroke survivors following hospital discharge. Benefits to stroke survivors were previously reported (Melifonwu, 2019). This research aimed to determine effectiveness of the LASC intervention.
Methods: Participants were randomized to usual care or LASC Program which consisted of Stroke Ambassadors-led group physical activity, stroke education, secondary prevention and psychosocial support. The LASC group attended two days/week for four hours/day. Blinded assessors assessed outcome measures at baseline and three months using modified Barthel Index, Stroke Impact Scale, Functional Independence Measure, EQ-5D-5L and functional goals.
Results: 55 participants per group (n=110) were recruited into the study. Analysis of data from Barthel index showed moderate improvements in the LASC group in physical function and self-care, mean difference 6.84; p=0.05 (95% confidence level: 0.01 to 13.69). Data from the EQ-5D-5L showed moderate improvements in health-related quality of life. Subtle changes only were noted in the control group participants and outcomes were not statistically significant.
Conclusions: The study demonstrated that improvements made by the LASC group could be attributed to interventions received in the LASC. Given that the participants randomized to intervention attend, and the sample size was small, this study demonstrates that larger effectiveness study is feasible.
EV479 / #1661
MINDFULNESS-BASED INSPIRATORY MUSCLE TRAINING FOR ENHANCING FUNCTIONAL OUTCOMES IN PEOPLE WITH STROKE: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL PROTOCOL
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.R. Hou1, A. Law1, J. Lee1, G. Ku1, J. Ko1, Y. Lee1, D. Sanchez-Vidana1, J. Zhang1, P. Kwong1, D. Yau1, S. Ngai1, M. Ying2, M. Pang1, T. Miller1
1The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Department Of Rehabilitation Sciences, Hong Kong, Hong Kong PRC, 2The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Department Of Health Technology And Informatics, Hong Kong, Hong Kong PRC
Background and Aims: Impaired central motor control may lead to contralateral diaphragmatic muscle weakness after stroke. It is estimated that approximately half of all stroke survivors experience poor respiratory control due to diaphragmatic dysfunction. Impaired respiratory control may exacerbate functional declines and mental health issues following stroke. This single-blind randomized control trial will assess the efficacy of a novel mindfulness-based inspiratory muscle training (MB-IMT) intervention for enhancing exercise tolerance, maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP) and mental health in people with chronic stroke.
Methods: Participants will be randomly allocated to either an MB-IMT intervention or inspiratory muscle training (IMT) alone. Both MB-IMT and IMT interventions will involve 24 face-to-face sessions and 16 home-based practice sessions over an 8-week period. Primary outcomes measured at baseline and at 8-week follow-up will include: (1) exercise tolerance assessed using the 6-minute walking test; (2) MIP assessed using full-body plethysmography and (3) mental health status using the Hamilton Depression Rating and General Anxiety Disorder-7 scales.
Results: We anticipate the study findings will not only improve our understanding of the relationship between physical and psychological (i.e., mind-body) aspects of post-stroke recovery but may also provide clinicians with a more efficient, comprehensive, and individually tailored treatment strategy for managing stroke-related respiratory dysfunction.
Conclusions: The findings will help inform clinical practice and guide future trials involving larger cohorts. Insights gained will also enhance current stroke recovery programs for various stakeholders within the local community. The results are expected to offer important evidence which can facilitate the development and integration of feasible, scalable, and cost-effective mind-body interventions.
EV480 / #1703
USING TECHNOLOGY-ASSISTED MATCHING PARADIGMS FOR EVALUATING UPPER LIMB PROPRIOCEPTION AFTER STROKE: A SCOPING REVIEW
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.G. Gu1, R. Lin2, R. Zeng2, R. Hou2, L. Chen3, D. Sanchez-Vidana2, P. Kwong2, K. Fong2, M. Pang2, T. Miller2, J. Zhang2
1Dongguan People’s Hospital, Department Of Rehabilitation, Dongguan, China, 2The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Department Of Rehabilitation Sciences, Hong Kong, Hong Kong PRC, 3The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, School Of Optometry, Hong Kong, Hong Kong PRC
Background and Aims: Loss of proprioception and kinesthesia negatively impacts motor recovery, functional independence and the ability to perform activities of daily living following stroke. It is estimated that between 34-64% of stroke survivors experience impaired proprioception. This scoping review aimed to synthesize the available literature on (1) the use of technology-assisted matching paradigms for assessing upper limb proprioceptive ability in people with stroke and (2) examine the psychometric properties of the assessments used.
Methods: A systematic search of MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science databases was performed from their respective inceptions to the current date. Studies evaluating the psychometric properties of proprioceptive assessments involving matching paradigms (i.e., the ability to achieve/reproduce a target joint position) and technological assistance (e.g., motion sensors, robotics) in people with stroke were considered for inclusion. Study quality was determined using the QUADAS-2 tool.
Results: Thirteen articles were included. Robot-assisted upper limb mirror-matching tasks were the most frequently used assessments (n=9). Assessments demonstrated moderate concurrent validity (n=7), and moderate convergent validity (n=4). Assessments also showed moderate to high inter-rater and test-retest reliability (n=5). Studies involving people with stroke and healthy comparators demonstrated good responsiveness (n=7).
Conclusions: This review provides a novel synthesis of the current literature evaluating the use of technology-assisted matching paradigms for assessing upper limb proprioception post-stroke. Reported reliability or validity ranged from moderate to high in various clinical settings. Responsiveness was also good. A comprehensive investigation of the psychometric properties of technologically-assisted matching paradigms which involving larger participant cohorts is warranted.
EV481 / #1797
EFFICACY OF CEREBROLYSIN COMBINED WITH EXTENDED REHABILITATION ON UPPER LIMB RECOVERY IN SEVERE SUBACUTE STROKE: AN ONGOING RANDOMIZED CLINICAL TRIAL
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.S. Mitrovic1, O. Djordjevic1, A. Vidakovic1, Z. Bukumiric2, S. Dedijer Dujovic1, T. Dimkic Tomic1, A. Radic1, L. Konstantinovic1
1Faculty of Medicine University of Belgrade, Belgrade, Serbia; Clinic for Rehabilitation "dr Miroslav Zotovic", Belgrade, Serbia, Neurorehabilitation, Belgrade, Serbia, 2Faculty of Medicine University of Belgrade, Belgrade, Serbia;Institute for Medical Statistics and Informatics Belgrade, Serbia, Belgrade, Serbia
Background and Aims: Previous studies suggest that administering Cerebrolysin during the early phase of stroke, in combination with rehabilitation, may improve outcomes and reduce mortality in patients with severe stroke. This study aimed to assess the efficacy of extended post-stroke rehabilitation combined with Cerebrolysin on upper limb motor recovery in early subacute stroke patients with severe motor impairment.
Methods: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 77 subacute stroke patients were assigned to receive either Cerebrolysin or placebo (n=40Cerebrolysin; Placebo=37). All patients underwent three weeks of daily conventional rehabilitation, followed by sessions three times weekly until day 90. The primary outcome was the Action Research Arm Test (ARAT); secondary outcomes included Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity (FMA-UE), Barthel Index (BI), and NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS). Assessments were done at baseline, after three weeks, and at day 90. No adverse events occurred; one patient in the Cerebrolysin group dropped out.
Results: Both groups showed significant improvement in ARAT and FMA-UE scores over time. However, the Cerebrolysin group improved more than the control group, significantly at week 3 (ARAT: p=0.02; FMA-UE: p=0.48) and day 90 (ARAT: p=0.00; FMA-UE: p=0.04). Statistical tests included t-test, Mann-Whitney, and Fisher exact test, with significance set at p<0.05.
Conclusions: Cerebrolysin led to greater improvement in post-stroke upper limb motor function compared to placebo, as measured by ARAT and FMA-UE, with significant effects observed after three weeks and sustained at 90 days. This effect may be attributed to Cerebrolysin’s multimodal impact on long-term neuroregeneration mechanisms, enhanced by extended neurorehabilitation.
EV482 / #790
ENHANCING UPPER LIMB RECOVERY IN STROKE PATIENTS THROUGH TRANSCRANIAL MAGNETIC STIMULATION AND OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.L. Molina, C. Márquez, C. Carbonero, R. Bragulat, M. Vallejos, M. Ochoa, S. Delgado-Gallén, R. Pelayo-Vergara
Fundació Institut Guttmann, Barcelona, Spain
Background and Aims: Stroke is a major cause of upper limb (UL) motor disability. Repetitive transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS), combined with occupational therapy (OT), has shown potential in improving neuroplasticity and recovery. This study aimed to assess the safety and effectiveness of an rTMS-OT program and how patient characteristics influence UL recovery.
Methods: Ten patients (40% women, mean age 60.5 years, SD = 10.57) participated in the study, which included 90% thrombotic ischemic and 10% hemorrhagic stroke, of whom 20% had infratentorial lesions. The mean time since the lesion was 43.8 months (SD = 40.15), and 70% had left hemisphere damage. Functional changes were assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment scale (FMA) and Stroke Upper Limb Capacity Scale (SULCS). Treatment consisted of rTMS applied to the non-affected hemisphere (1 Hz, 1500 pulses, inhibitory protocol), followed by one hour of OT focused on functional patterns,mirror therapy,manipulative dexterity, and UL integration into daily activities. Pre- and post-treatment differences were analyzed using t-tests, while ANOVA examined the impact of patient characteristics.
Results: UL functional prognosis improved from 40% to 60%. Significant gains were observed in FMA (p = 0.002) and SULCS (p = 0.017). ANOVA showed no significant impact of time since the lesion, initial prognosis, affected side, or cortical involvement (p > 0.05), but gender significantly influenced SULCS (F = 11.815, p = 0.009).
Conclusions: The combination of rTMS and OT is safe and effective for UL recovery in post-stroke patients. It is independent of lesion timing or initial prognosis. However,larger studies are needed to validate these findings.
EV483 / #1436
SEX-SPECIFIC CARDIORESPIRATORY FITNESS PERFORMANCE ON AN ADAPTIVE RECUMBENT STEPPER EXERCISE TEST IN PEOPLE POST-STROKE
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.K. Moncion1,2, L. Rodrigues1,2, B. De Las Heras De Miguel1,2,3, E. Wiley4,5, K. Sikorska1,2, J. Cristini1,2, E. Allison6, J.J. Eng7, A. Tang8, M. Roig1,2
1McGill University, School Of Physical & Occupational Therapy, Montreal, Canada, 2Jewish Rehabilitation Hospital, Memory And Motor Rehabilitation Laboratory, Laval, Canada, 3Cereneo Center for Neurology & Rehabilitation, Weggis, Switzerland, 4University of British Columbia, Department Of Occupational Sciences And Occupational Therapy, Kelowna, Canada, 5University of British Columbia, Centre For Chronic Disease Prevention And Management, Kelowna, Canada, 6McMaster University, Kinesiology, Hamilton, Canada, 7University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, 8McMaster University, Hamilton, Canada
Background and Aims: Cardiopulmonary exercise tests (CPET) are a key component of aerobic exercise prescription after stroke, yet sex-specific cardiorespiratory fitness data are lacking. This study characterized the sex-specific cardiorespiratory fitness performance on a recumbent stepper CPET in people across the continuum of stroke recovery.
Methods: Individuals with subacute (⩽ 3 months) and chronic (⩾ 6 months) stroke underwent a symptom-limited recumbent stepper CPET. Each CPET was assessed for ventilatory threshold (VT, mL/kg/min), peak oxygen uptake (V̇O2peak, mL/kg/min) and achievement of maximal (V̇O2max) criterion standards, such as achieving: 1) a Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) ⩾1.10; 2) Ratings of Perceived Exertion (RPE) ⩾17/20 or ⩾7/10, 3) a V̇O2 plateau, 4) peak heart rate (HR) within 10 beats of maximal HR. T-tests, rank-sum tests, Chi-squared, or Fisher’s exact tests were used to evaluate sex differences by stroke acuity.
Results: Sixty-nine subacute (n=20 females, 2.1 ± 0.8 months post-stroke) and seventy-six chronic (n=25 females, 1.7 ± 1.2 years post-stroke) stroke survivors were tested. In subacute stroke, there no were no differences in VT or V̇O2peak (p>0.05), but females were more likely to achieve a V̇O2 plateau (p=0.002). In chronic stroke, no differences were observed for VT or any V̇O2max criterion (p>0.05), but females had lower V̇O2peak (p=0.002). Overall, the most achieved V̇O2max criterion was RPE (n=79, 55%) and RER (n=67, 46%), with participants meeting one (n=70, 48%) or meeting two (n=42, 29%) criterion.
Conclusions: Despite sex differences in CPET performance, the achievement of V̇O2max is low and dependent on the criterion post-stroke.
EV484 / #1663
A NOVEL PCA-BASED MOTOR-MOBILITY SCORE: A SUBANALYSIS OF THE PHYS-STROKE TRIAL
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.A. Nave1, K. Neumann2, T. Rackoll1
1Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Clinic For Neurology, Berlin, Germany, 2Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Institute Of Biostatistics, Berlin, Germany
Background and Aims: Randomised trials in stroke rehabilitation often assess recovery using a single outcome, which may oversimplify complex recovery trajectories. In the domain of mobility, for example, patients may improve in walking speed while remaining limited in functional capacity. We propose a novel motor-mobility score (MMS) to capture more nuanced recovery, and apply it to data from the multicentre, randomised controlled PHYS-STROKE trial (Nave et al., BMJ, 2019).
Methods: In PHYS-STROKE, subacute stroke patients (n=200) receiving inpatient rehabilitation were followed up at three and six months post-stroke. We developed a principal component analysis (PCA)-based composite MMS using four metrics: maximal walking speed, 6-minute walking distance, lower limb strength (MRC scale), and Rivermead Motor Assessment (arm). Recovery over six months was analysed using multiple regression to identify associations with baseline characteristics.
Results: The PCA-derived MMS offers a continuous and sensitive measure of motor-mobility recovery, surpassing traditional binary responder classifications. MMS improved between baseline and follow-up in 92.6% of the relaxation group and 90.5% of the training group (p=0.770). Greater MMS improvements at six months were associated with lower baseline NT-proBNP (p=0.005), lower HbA1c (p=0.002), younger age (p=0.055), and lower admission NIHSS scores (p=0.005). Additionally, patients with higher admission NIHSS recovered more between three to six months post stroke (p=0.003).
Conclusions: The MMS enables nuanced, continuous analysis of motor and mobility recovery post-stroke. Patients with lower cardiometabolic risk at baseline experienced better functional mobility outcomes.
EV485 / #1372
CAN TRAINING OF NON-AFFECTED LEG WITH ECCENTRIC OVERLOAD TECHNIQUE IMPROVE MUSCLE FUNCTION, BALANCE, WALKING ABILITY AND PERCEIVED PARTICIPATION IN CHRONIC STROKE SUBJECTS?
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.C. Nissemark1, P. Sojka2, B. Åslund2
1University of Umeå, Faculty Of Medicin, Umeå, Sweden, 2Östersunds Rehabcentrum, Östersund Hospital, Östersund, Östersund, Sweden
Background and Aims: The purpose of this study was to investigate effects of training of the non-affected leg
with coupled concentric and eccentric contractions, including eccentric overload, on strength
in the non-affected and the affected leg as well as on some aspects of motor performance.
Methods: Nine chronic stroke subjects performed eccentric overload training with non-
affected leg, 2 times per week during 8 weeks. Flywheel leg press resistance exercise device
(YoYo Tecchnology AB,Stockholm, Sweden) Peak power, isometric leg press force and
training data were measured during all training sessions. Aspects of balance, gait and
movement performance were assessed using appropriate tests before and after the training
period of 8 weeks.
Results: Peak power measured during training increased between session 1 and 16 for both
concentric (12.7% <0.001) and eccentric action (13.4% p<0.001) for the trained non-
affected leg. Peak power in the affected leg increased for both concentric (22 %, p=0.028)
and eccentric action (38 %, p=0.015). Timed-up-and-go (14 %, p=0.021), Berg balance test

EXPERIENCES OF STROKE SURVIVORS WITH SPATIAL NEGLECT: A QUALITATIVE SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.A. Oki-Golovkina1, G. Fisher2, C. Ryan3, B. Turtle4, T. Stapleton5, A. Porter-Armstrong3, N. Hassanzadeh1, D. Kennedy1
1University of Victoria, Exercise Science, Physical And Health Education, Victoria, Canada, 2Macquarie University, Sydney, Australia, 3Edinburgh Napier University, Edinburgh, United Kingdom, 4Ulster University, Derry, United Kingdom, 5Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland
Background and Aims: Spatial neglect (SN) is common after a stroke. SN results in the misperception of stimuli opposite to the lesion. Quality patient-centred care relies on input from those with lived-experience and is essential for making healthcare decisions. We aimed to review the literature on patients’ experiences with SN, particularly assessment and management, as part of a larger study exploring both patient and clinician perspectives on SN.
Methods: We conducted a systematic review following JBI methodology for qualitative evidence synthesis. Five databases were searched until April 2024 using terms related to stroke, spatial neglect, and patient/clinician experience. Four independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts, and two reviewers screened full texts. Data were extracted using JBI SUMARI and methodological quality was assessed using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Findings were synthesized via meta-aggregation with discrepancies resolved through discussion until consensus was reached.
Results: 819 papers were initially screened, with only seven meeting the inclusion/exclusion criteria for patient experiences. Six categories emerged from the synthesis of the included studies: 1) anosognosia for neglect; 2) unawareness of neglect; 3) altered awareness of the body; 4) developing intellectual awareness of neglect; 5) impact of neglect on quality of life; 6) strategies to reduce neglect.
Conclusions: Unsurprisingly, patients with SN experienced misperception of the left world, often without realizing the extent of their impairments. Significantly, no results linked assessment of neglect to awareness of the condition or management strategies, highlighting a critical gap between clinical assessment practices and patients’ lived experiences.

EXPERIENCES OF CLINICIANS ASSESSING AND TREATING SPATIAL NEGLECT POST-STROKE: A QUALITATIVE SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.A. Oki-Golovkina1, G. Fisher2, C. Ryan3, B. Turtle4, T. Stapleton5, A. Porter-Armstrong3, N. Hassanzadeh1, D. Kennedy1
1University of Victoria, Exercise Science, Physical And Health Education, Victoria, Canada, 2Macquarie University, Sydney, Australia, 3Edinburgh Napier University, Edinburgh, United Kingdom, 4Ulster University, Derry, United Kingdom, 5Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland
Background and Aims: Spatial neglect (SN) affects ~40% of people after stroke. Effective management requires clinical expertise and understanding of how clinicians navigate challenges in complex healthcare settings. Despite clinicians’ critical role, research exploring their experiences is limited. This review synthesized the literature on clinicians’ experiences with SN assessment and treatment, as part of a larger study exploring patient and clinician perspectives on SN.
Methods: This systematic review followed JBI methodology for qualitative evidence synthesis. Five databases were searched until April 2024 using terms related to stroke, spatial neglect, and patient/clinician experience. Four independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts, and two reviewers screened full texts. Data were extracted using JBI SUMARI and methodological quality was assessed using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Findings were synthesized via meta-aggregation with discrepancies resolved through discussion until consensus was reached.
Results: From 819 initially screened papers, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria for clinician experiences. INTEROCEPTIVE ALTERATIONS IN POST-STROKE INDIVIDUALS: A COMPARATIVE CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY
REHABILITATION AND LIFE AFTER STROKE.M. Ozgun1,2, O. Akanyeti3, F. Villagra Povina3, B. Dal Koyuncuoglu2
1Bogazici University, Institute Of Biomedical Engineering, Istanbul, Turkey, 2Istanbul Health and Technology University, Physiotherapy And Rehabilitation, Istanbul, Turkey, 3Aberystwyth University, Department Of Computer Science, Ceredigion, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Interoception refers to the complex neurophysiological process of sensing, integrating, and modeling visceral and somatic inputs to generate real-time internal state monitoring which is crucial for homeostasis and adaptive cognitive-emotional responses. Within the framework of the allostatic interoception model, this internal sensing system not only reacts to current physiological demands but also predicts and prepares for anticipated needs. Discrepancies between predicted and actual interoceptive signals may cause allostatic overload, disrupting neural signalling. So far, very few studies have investigated whether stroke impairs interoceptive networks and how these impairments are associated with cognitive and motor functions. This study, therefore, aimed to investigate interoceptive capacity in post-stoke individuals.
Methods: Forty stroke patients with Mini-Mental Test scores of >25 were compared with forty healthy controls with similar age and sex distribution. Interoceptive dimensions were assessed through Heartbeat-Detection Task for interoceptive accuracy, Interoceptive Sensory Scale for subjective sensitivity, and Toronto Alexithymia Scale for interoceptive awareness. Cognitive performance was evaluated with Trail-Making Test, while motor functioning was assessed with Fugl-Meyer Motor Scale.
Results: demonstrated significantly reduced interoceptive accuracy, sensitivity and elevated alexithymia scores in the stroke group compared to controls (p=0.018, p=0.043, p=0.038 respectively). No significant association was observed between interoception and motor performance. However, interoceptive accuracy was positively correlated with cognitive function (r=0.248, p=0.037).
Conclusions: Our findings indicate that stroke-related neurophysiological alterations may deteriorate interoceptive function. Incorporating interoceptive assessments and targeted interventions into clinical rehabilitation may improve recovery outcomes. Further research is needed to clarify the contribution of interoceptive dysfunction to post-stroke cognitive and emotional impairments.

Results: A total of 30 participants were included in the study. Participants who displayed apathy and passivity’s attitudes seemed to be based on the skepticism, unreadiness and negative attitude towards technology interventions. While those who expressed Optimism and Positivity reflected on the accessibility, convenience and continuity of care that telerehabilitation afforded.
Conclusions: The attitudes of the healthcare providers towards telerehabilitation were both positive and negative. The findings should be taken into consideration when designing telerehabilitation programmes for stroke survivors living in low-resourced settings.

Background and Aims: Stroke frequently leads to upper limb motor impairments, substantially affecting functional independence. Conventional therapy often falls short in intensity and engagement. Game-based rehabilitation using biomimetic pathways—trajectories mimicking natural inter-joint coordination—may enhance motor recovery. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of predefined versus randomized biomimetic control mechanisms in game-based rehabilitation on upper limb motor function and activity in stroke patients.
Methods: A single-centre pilot randomized controlled trial was conducted at Kasturba Hospital, Manipal. Twenty participants with unilateral stroke were randomized to receive either predefined (n=10) or randomized (n=10) biomimetic movement pathways using the ArmAble™ device. Outcomes—Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity (FMA-UE), Action Research Arm Test (ARAT), and reach velocity—were assessed at baseline, day 3, day 6, and one-week post-intervention. 1Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, National Resource Centre For Value Education In Engineering (nrcvee), New Delhi, India, 2All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, Department Of Neurology, New Delhi, India, 3All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, Department Of Neurology, New Delhi, India, 4Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Department Of Civil Engineering & National Resource Centre For Value Education In Engineering (nrcvee), New Delhi, India, 5Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Department Of Computer Science And Engineering & National Resource Centre For Value Education In Engineering (nrcvee), New Delhi, India

Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted to identify empirical studies involving non-English adaptations of MIT in individuals with PSNFA that assessed language outcomes (PROSPERO: CRD42022364449). EXPLORING THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ABNORMAL INTERMUSCULAR COORDINATION AND JOINT TORQUE COUPLING: INSIGHTS FOR POST-STROKE REHABILITATION

1University of Houston, Biomedical Engineering, Houston, United States of America, 2Rice University, Mechanical Engineering, Houston, United States of America, 3TIRR Memorial Hermann, Houston, United States of America
Background and Aims: Abnormal joint torque coupling, such as involuntary elbow flexion during shoulder abduction (flexor synergy), and disrupted muscle synergy composition are common motor impairments after stroke. While both phenomena are well-documented, their relationship remains unexplored. This study aimed to examine whether greater joint torque coupling is associated with greater disruption in muscle synergy composition in the hemiparetic upper extremity.
Methods: Five healthy individuals (age: 38.9 ± 9.1 years) and five stroke survivors (56.5 ± 6.1) performed two tasks: (1) an isometric force target-reaching task to assess muscle synergies and (2) a torque generation task isolating shoulder abduction. Surface EMG was recorded from eight upper limb muscles. Muscle synergies were extracted using non-negative matrix factorization, and a similarity index was computed relative to healthy controls. Torque coupling was defined as the ratio of unintended elbow flexion torque (secondary) to intended shoulder abduction torque (primary).
Results: A strong negative correlation was found between muscle synergy similarity and torque coupling during should abduction (R² = 0.802, p < 0.05, Figure. 1). This suggests that greater synergy disruption is associated with more abnormal torque coupling. Other joint conditions showed weaker or non-significant associations.

Conclusions: This study provides novel evidence linking post-stroke neuromuscular coordination deficits with biomechanical impairments in joint torque control. The finding supports the need for integrative rehabilitation strategies targeting both muscle synergy restoration and biomechanical normalization to improve motor recovery in stroke survivors.

This study systematically evaluates the comparative effectiveness of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), theta burst stimulation (TBS) and transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) in enhancing brain excitability, upper limb and overall motor functions after stroke.
Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science to identify one meta-analysis for each intervention. Most recent reviews clearly presenting the effect sizes of above interventions were selected.
Results: In total, four reviews were included. The analysis suggests that all brain stimulation interventions contribute to stroke recovery. Among the five interventions, VNS and TBS have demonstrated highest impact on motor function, with standardized mean difference in Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA) scores of 2.14[1.32, 3.45] and 2.70[-0.02, 5.42], respectively. TUS and TMS also showed positive effects, with effect sizes of 0.98[0.45, 1.52] and 0.63[0.42, 0.85], respectively. However, the safety profile of TUS appears to be better than others. VNS and TMS may cause adverse events, while no side effects have been reported for TUS to date.
Conclusions: In conclusion, DCS, VNS, TBS, TUS and TMS have demonstrated effectiveness in motor function recovery after stroke. However, the data is limited, and it requires further clinical investigation to establish an optimal non-invasive intervention. In all five meta-analyses, the efficacy was assessed mostly for immediate effect with longest up to 90-days. Long term safety and efficacy of the stimulation techniques remain unclear.

MANAGEMENT OF EARLY NEUROLOGICAL DETERIORATION IN LACUNAR INFARCTS

1Fleni, Neurology, Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2FLENI, Neurocritical Care Unit, Buenos Aires, Argentina
Background and Aims: Early neurological deterioration (END) in lacunar infarcts is a significant complication occurring usually in the first five days post-stroke, despite initial treatment. END mechanisms remain unclear, and no standardized management protocol exists. This study aims to describe the clinical presentation, predictors, and management of END in small-vessel disease (SVD)-related ischemic strokes and assess their impact on functional outcomes.
Methods: This single-center, retrospective, observational study analyzed 269 patients with acute lacunar strokes from 2013 to 2023. END was defined as symptom fluctuation or progression during hospitalization. Demographic, clinical, imaging, and therapeutic data were collected, and functional outcomes were evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at 90 days. Statistical comparisons were conducted to identify predictors of END and assess therapeutic interventions.
Results: END occurred in 32 patients (11.9%), characterized as fluctuations (81%) or progressions (19%). Lesions in the internal capsule and lenticular nucleus were more frequent in the END group. Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel) and hemodynamic optimization were employed in most cases, yielding a high rate of favorable outcomes. Predictive analyses identified no significant associations with vascular risk factors, but lesion location and size were critical determinants.
Conclusions: END in lacunar strokes remains a challenging complication. Dual antiplatelet therapy and hemodynamic optimization appear effective strategies to mitigate progression and improve outcomes. Background and Aims: This study aimed to elucidate the characteristics and mechanisms of spontaneous nystagmus violating the Alexander’s law.

Twenty patients with vestibular neuritis served as a control. We also implemented a mathematical model to simulate the nystagmus violating Alexander’s law.
Results: Patients showed a violation of Alexander’s law in one or both directions of lateral gaze. When Alexander’s law is violated, the Tc was larger than that in the controls (median [IQR]: 14.4 s [6.4-38.9] vs 9.0 s [5.5-12.6], p=0.036) while the Tc did not differ between the groups when Alexander’ law is obeyed (9.6 s [3.6-16.1] vs 9.0 s [5.5-12.6], p=0.924). In a mathematical model with normal integrator function, the false rotational cue generates nystagmus following Alexander’s law. The first lesion, which changes the brainstem neural integrator, and the second lesion, which causes the Purkinje synapse to exert excitatory input, both lead to nystagmus that violates Alexander’s law.
Conclusions: We propose that when the neural integrator is unstable with lesions in the brainstem neural integrator itself or the neural synapse between Purkinje cells and the brainstem vestibular nucleus, nystagmus violates Alexander’s law.

Background and Aims: Temperature-related vascular stress is an underrecognized contributor to acute cerebrovascular events. Sudden environmental temperature shifts, particularly from cold to warm, can provoke dramatic changes in vascular tone and blood pressure. These physiological responses may trigger ischemic strokes, especially in individuals with predisposing cardiovascular risk factors.
Methods: We present two unique cases illustrating stroke onset following abrupt temperature transitions. The first involves a 39-year-old male with a high BMI, dyslipidemia, and a history of migraines, who developed acute cerebellar stroke symptoms after engaging in intense physical activity followed by an ice bath. Imaging revealed an acute left cerebellar infarction, with no evidence of arterial dissection.
The second case features a 55-year-old hypertensive, heavy-smoking security guard who developed stroke symptoms after prolonged exposure to sub-zero temperatures, followed by sudden rewarming in a heated office. MRI confirmed an acute left pontine infarct.
Results: In both cases, the sequence of vasodilation (from exercise or cold-induced adaptation) followed by sudden vasoconstriction or rewarming likely triggered rapid blood pressure fluctuations and sympathetic activation. This may have precipitated thrombotic events through mechanisms such as increased vascular resistance, endothelial dysfunction, and hypercoagulability.
Conclusions: These cases highlight temperature-related vascular stress as a potential stroke trigger, particularly during abrupt cold-to-warm transitions. Heightened clinical awareness is needed, especially in at-risk populations exposed to extreme environmental or physiological conditions. Further research is warranted to elucidate preventive strategies in temperature-sensitive cerebrovascular events. MRI scans for our patients.

ROLE OF PROVOCATIVE DIGITAL SUBTRACTION ANGIOGRAM (DSA) FOR DIAGNOSIS OF RECURRENT ISCHEMIC STROKES IN POSTERIOR CIRCULATION
STROKE IN THE YOUNG AND UNCOMMON ETIOLOGIES.S. Ansari, M. Niemeyer, E. Greenberg, P. Tahsili Fahadan, R. Balu
Inova Health System, Neuroscience, Falls Church, United States of America
Background and Aims: We present a patient who suffered recurrent posterior circulation strokes due to dissection and thrombus from mechanical impingement of vertebral artery due to a malpositioned cervical pedicle screw.
Methods: 62-yo male with stroke risk factors and prior cervical fusions presented with dysarthria and right sided hemiparesis. CT head was negative for acute findings. CTA of head and neck showed left intracranial VA severe stenosis-or-occlusion; also concerning for hardware loosening from prior C1-T2 fusion, particularly malpositioning and lucency around C1 screws. MRI found scattered acute infarcts in posterior circulation. He was started on DAPT. Stroke work-up was otherwise unremarkable. Follow-up CT angiogram showed small filling defect within the intracranial left VA; larger than initial CT angiogram. No new strokes on MRI. With thrombus elongation, his medication was changed to apixaban and aspirin. Patient presented with transient recurrent symptoms; there were no new infarcts on imaging. His latest MRI showed new left cerebellum infarct despite maximal medical management. Dissection was suspected due to external pressure from malpositioned pedicle screw.
Results: Provocative DSA confirmed dissection of intracranial left VA. Left VA occluded when the head was turned either left or right due to cervical screw pressure, with flow restoration when head was in neutral position. Patient underwent malpositioned hardware removal and occiput to T2 fusion. Follow-up provocative DSA demonstrated healing of the dissection and no flow compromise with head version.
Conclusions: To highlight the utility of provocative DSA in diagnosis and treatment of patients with recurrent posterior circulation strokes despite unremarkable stroke workup and adequate medical management.

A CASE REPORT: NEUROPSYCHIATRIC AND SEIZURE MANIFESTATIONS IN MOYAMOYA DISEASE
STROKE IN THE YOUNG AND UNCOMMON ETIOLOGIES.M.F. Cabalu, R. Alvarez
MAKATI MEDICAL CENTER, Neurology, MAKATI, Philippines
Background and Aims: Moyamoya Disease (MMD) is a rare vasculopathy characterized by progressive stenosis of the distal segments of the internal carotid arteries, proximal middle, and anterior cerebral arteries are the most frequently affected, leading to ischemic events and subsequent collateral vessel development. While commonly recognized for ischemic strokes and transient ischemic attacks, MMD may present with varied neurological manifestations, including neuropsychiatric symptoms and seizures.
Methods: This is a case report of a 38-year-old male who presented with focal aware seizures, behavioral changes, and mood disturbances. Imaging showed bilateral Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) Occlusion.
Results: A 38 year old male right handed, Filipino presenting with a two week history of auditory hallucinations of hearing lyrics,de-ja-vu, and bilateral to generalized stiffening and jerking of extremities lasting for less than two minutes. This progressed to behavioral and mood changes described as combative, aggressive, and irritable behavior. MRI was unremarkable but MRA and CT perfusion showed bilateral MCA occlusion seen in Moyamoya Disease. He had one episode of new onset facial asymmetry during his admission and initially managed with Levetiracetam and Valproic Acid. The patient underwent Extracranial-Intracranial Bypass, left (Superior Temporal Artery- Middle Cerebral Artery M4 segment Anastomosis) with Encephalogaleosynangiosis. On the 9th hospital day, there was significant improvement of behavior and no recurrence of seizures. He was started on Aspirin 80mg once a day and discharged stable.
Conclusions: This case highlights the awareness of recognizing neuropsychiatric manifestations of Moyamoya Disease. Clinicians may consider MMD in young adults presenting with unexplained seizures and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

THE AGE DIVIDE: UNCOVERING THE DISTINCT FACES OF ISCHEMIC STROKE IN THE DOMINICAN REPUBLIC
STROKE IN THE YOUNG AND UNCOMMON ETIOLOGIES.S. Lora1, S. Castro2, M. Cedeño-Bruzual1, R. Romano3, E. Luna4, F. Méndez5, L. Suazo4
1CEDIMAT, Research Fellow, Neurology, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, 2CEDIMAT, Second Year Resident, Neurology, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, 3CEDIMAT, Scientific Research Coordinator, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, 4CEDIMAT, Coordinator, Stroke Unit, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, 5CEDIMAT, Medical Coordinator, Emergency Department, Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
Background and Aims: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) predominantly affects older adults, but early-onset cases are increasing. In the Dominican Republic (DR), this group remains understudied. We compared the etiology, severity, treatment, outcomes, and mortality between AIS patients aged <50 versus ⩾50 years.
Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study focuses on AIS patients treated at a DR stroke unit (July 2022 - March 2025), including 64 cases <50 years, sex-matched (1:1) to controls ⩾50 years. Demographics, TOAST classification, NIHSS, and mRS scales were summarized and analyzed using Mann-Whitney U tests (p<0.05) to compare outcomes.
Results: Median age was 31 years (IQR 31–49) in the <50 group and 74 (IQR 62.75–96) in those ⩾50. Among younger patients, cryptogenic stroke was most common (43.75%), followed by other determined etiologies (25.0%; mainly hypercoagulable states), large artery atherosclerosis (15.63%), and cardioembolism (15.63%). Conversely, patients ⩾50 primarily had large artery atherosclerosis (48.44%), cryptogenic stroke (32.81%), and cardioembolism (17.19%); no other determined etiologies were reported. Median admission NIHSS was lower in the younger group (3 versus 5), with similar revascularization rates between groups (p=0.38). Discharge mRS was lower in those <50 years (1 versus 2.4), while poor outcomes (mRS ⩾3) were significantly more frequent in the ⩾50 years group (45.31% versus 28.13%; p=0.012). Mortality occurred in 7.8% of patients ⩾50 years, with no deaths in younger patients.

Conclusions: While younger AIS patients had milder strokes and better outcomes, their broader etiologic profile —dominated by cryptogenic and rare causes— highlights the need for age-specific diagnostic and management strategies, particularly in regions with limited healthcare resources.

1All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, Neurology, New Delhi, India, 2Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Neurology, Chandigarh, India, 3All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Neuroimaging And Interventional Neuroradiology, New Delhi, India, 4Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education & Research, Internal Medicine, Chandigarh, India
Background and Aims: Ischemic stroke or cerebral infarction is a serious complication of tuberculous meningitis (TBM) and results from vasculitis, intimal proliferation, or a hypercoagulable state, affecting small- and medium-caliber vessels.

Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, Neurology, Kolkata, India
Background and Aims: The disease presentation of Moyamoya angiopathy (MMA) is known to vary amongst different ethnicity. This study aimed at assessing the clinico-radiological profile of MMA in the largest cohort of MMA patients in India.

The commonest type of MMA was cerebral infarction(48.9%). Gyral pattern were commoner in children(p=0.001). Stage 4(32.6%) and stage 5(30%) were the commonest Suzuki staging observed. Involvement of posterior circulation was detected in 55.1%. 64.0% had brain atrophy at the time of diagnosis, significantly associated with increased diagnostic latency(p<0.001).
Conclusions: Clinico-radiological features of Indian MMA share several dissimilarities to its Japanese and Caucasian counterparts. MMA is a frequently overlooked due to its myriad of transient neurological symptoms, often leading to delayed diagnosis. Subtle transient neurological symptoms (seizure or headache), along with cognitive decline and disproportionate radiological burden to the number of acute vascular events should raise suspicion for MMA.

BASILAR ARTERY FENESTRATIONS AND ISCHEMIC STROKE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF CLINICAL IMPACT, MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES, AND SECONDARY PREVENTION
STROKE IN THE YOUNG AND UNCOMMON ETIOLOGIES.O. Gutiérrez Treviño1,2, J. Figueroa-Sanchez1,2, J.M. Escamilla-Garza1,2, H.R. Martínez1,2, L.A. Cantú-Martínez1,2, A. Del Bosque1, R. Rodriguez-Monroy1, M. Garcia-Zubizar1
1Tecnologico de Monterrey, Escuela De Medicina Y Ciencias De La Salud, Monterrey, Mexico, 2Institute of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Centro Médico Zambrano Hellion, Tecsalud, San Pedro Garza Garcia, Mexico
Background and Aims: Basilar artery fenestrations (BAFs) are congenital vascular anomalies that may disrupt local hemodynamics, potentially contributing to ischemic stroke. Their true clinical significance remains controversial, and standardized management strategies are lacking. This review aimed to evaluate the possible causal link between BAFs and ischemic strokes, outline primary treatment approaches, and assess secondary prevention measures.
Methods: A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251068486). EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies reporting ischemic strokes associated with BAF. Inclusion criteria comprised observational studies, case reports, and clinical trials in English or Spanish. Data were extracted on demographics, fenestration type, imaging findings, treatments, and outcomes.
Results: Thirteen studies met criteria, comprising 16 patients (mean age 51.4 ± 16.9 years; 75% male). All strokes involved basilar artery territories, and most BAFs were proximal (38%). While a definitive causal relationship could not be established, anatomical and clinical correlations suggest BAFs may contribute to stroke in select patients. Primary treatment varied and included intravenous thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, and anticoagulation. Secondary prevention most often consisted of antiplatelet therapy, with no reported recurrences among patients with follow-up.
Conclusions: Although causality between BAF and ischemic stroke remains unproven, their anatomical characteristics and stroke localization support a potential pathogenic role. Acute management aligns with standard stroke care. Secondary prevention with antiplatelets appears effective, though evidence is limited. Future studies should clarify the clinical significance of BAFs and define optimal long-term strategies.

WHEN STROKE MEETS CANCER: DIAGNOSTIC CLUES, ASSOCIATIONS AND THERAPEUTIC GAPS – EXPERIENCE FROM A LARGE DISTRICT GENERAL HOSPITAL IN THE UNITED KINGDOM
STROKE IN THE YOUNG AND UNCOMMON ETIOLOGIES.A. Ghafar, A. Ghafar, S. Das
New Cross Hospital, Stroke Medicine, Wolverhampton, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Ischaemic stroke and systemic cancer are closely linked. Unique pathogenesis including cancer hypercoagulability often presents with multi-territory infarctions. Our local project aimed to explore the clinical and radiological characteristics of cancer-associated strokes, along with the therapeutic challenges in this subtype.
Methods: Retrospective data from electronic records was collected from all stroke admissions from January to June 2024 at New Cross Hospital, Wolverhampton. Data on demographics, comorbidities, cancer work-up, biochemical investigations, imaging and treatment were analysed.
Results: Of 633 stroke admissions, 49 patients had acute ischaemic stroke alongside active or a history of cancer. The mean age was 74.3 years and sex ratio was 3:1.9. The main cardiovascular risk factors were hypertension (63.3%) and hyperlipidaemia (63.3%). Gastrointestinal malignancy was the commonest cancer type (28.3%). 51.9% of patients had stage 3 cancer or above, with 22.4% having had cancer treatment within 1 month prior to stroke diagnosis. Cortical stroke was noted to be more prevalent than non-cortical stroke. Multi-territory infarcts were found in 22.4% of cases. Within this cohort, a cardioembolic cause was present in 27.3% whilst the remaining 72.7% had no identifiable cause. Of patients with multi-territory infarcts and no identifiable cardioembolic phenomenon, treatment with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) was initiated in 12.5%.
Conclusions: Unexplained multi-territory infarcts should raise suspicion for underlying malignancy and prompt cancer screening. In patients with features suggestive of cancer-associated thrombosis and particularly ‘three-territory sign’, there is limited evidence on optimal treatment, but LMWH may be considered. Further studies to establish a standardised risk assessment and treatment are essential.

His medical history was remarkable for brain tumor diagnosed at 15 years of age with operation, radiation, and chemotherapy. Magnetic resonance (MR) images showed a new cerebral infarction in the pons and previous craniotomy at occipital bone, severe atrophy of bilateral cerebellum. MR angiography revealed severe stenoocclusive lesions at both distal vertebral arteries and multifocal stenosis with underlying hypoplastic change of basilary trunk. He was medically treated with active rehabilitation.

Results: Our presumptive diagnosis was pontine infarction secondary to late-onset radiation-induced vasculopathy. His stroke risk factor workup showed slightly elevated hemoglobin A1c (6.4%) and elevated low-density lipoprotein at 196 mg/dL, which were considered likely contributing factors.
Conclusions: Our patient’s presentation with stroke symptoms and imaging findings resembling the ischemic stroke commonly seen in older adults suggest that radiation combined with other risk factors (hyperlipidemia and diabetes) might accelerate the pathogenesis of large vessel disease. In young adult with history of brain tumor treated with radiation, identifying those at risk for delayed cerebrovascular complications is an important task. Measures to minimize radiation to the posterior fossa during treatment could potentially decrease long-term risk of radiation-induced vasculopathy and stroke in brain tumor survivors.

Background and Aims: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) causes inflammation of large blood vessels, usually in older adults, and rarely mimics transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), but recognizing it early is crucial to prevent serious complications.
Methods: A registered blind 69-year-old gentleman with albinism and a history of TIA, non-aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, and diabetes attended the hospital with a 3-hour history of headache, mild right-sided weakness, and mixed dysphasia. Results: The classic presentation of GCA with headache and visual symptoms can be easily overlooked in patients with visual impairment.
Conclusions: With CTA being widely available, any relevant findings should alert clinicians of the possibility of vasculitis in those presenting with headaches. A collaborative approach with the neuroradiologist and rheumatologist was key to optimal management.

STROKE IN THE YOUNG AND UNCOMMON ETIOLOGIES.N. Jahan, R. Palathinkal, A. Baheerathan

STROKE IN THE YOUNG AND UNCOMMON ETIOLOGIES.E. Jasukaitiene1, R. Radisauskas1, A. Tamosiunas1, L. Sileikiene1, D. Kranciukaite-Butylkiniene1, S. Augustis1, D. Luksiene1, K. Marcinkeviciene1, D. Zaliaduonyte2, G. Sakalyte1,2

Background and Aims: Reliable data on stroke trends are critical for guiding public health interventions. Background and Aims: Tandem arterial anterior circulation intracranial occlusions (TO) are acute ischemic strokes (AIS) that involve an extra-cranial carotid lesion (ECL) with severe stenosis or total occlusion of the internal carotid artery (ICA) with an intracranial vessel occlusion. TOs were excluded and underrepresented in most of the randomized controlled trials (RCT). There is no scientific evidence on how to treat the ECL from RCT. The Proximal Internal Carotid Artery Acute Stroke Secondary to Tandem or Local Occlusion (PICASSO) Thrombectomy Trial, aims to evaluate whether acute carotid stenting or non-stenting management leads to better patient functional outcomes.
Methods: The PICASSO Trial is a prospective, phase III, randomized, open-label, blinded-endpoint controlled trial (PROBE Design), with planned enrollment of 404 patients. Patients will be randomized 1:1 into either mechanical thrombectomy plus extracranial carotid stenting (MT+CAS) or MT plus non-stenting methods (MT+CAT). The primary efficacy endpoint is the 90-day mRS ordinal shift analysis of functional patient outcomes, and the primary safety endpoint is the rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage at 24 hours.
Results: The first patient was enrolled in the PICASSO Trial on May 8th, 2024. At the time of submitting this abstract, 86 patients have been enrolled across 48 active sites in the US. The first DSMB meeting, at 50 patients, concluded no safety concerns and to continue the study as designed. The first pre-planned interim analysis at 101 is expected in the Fall of 2025.
Conclusions: A comprehensive overview and update on the ongoing PICASSO Trial will be provided at the World Stroke Conference late-breaking abstract session.

CEREBRAL AIR EMBOLISM AS A RARE COMPLICATION OF MECHANICAL THROMBECTOMY IN ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE
THROMBECTOMY.A. Ali1, A. Mathews1, W. Mohamed1, S. Shahid1, K. Zin1, A. Gregory1, T. Bakare1, M. Khan2
1North Bristol NHS Trust, Neuroscience Department, Bristol, United Kingdom, 2Queen Elizabeth Hospital, University Hospitals of Birmingham, Geriatrics, Bristol, United Kingdom
Background and Aims: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is a key treatment for acute ischemic stroke due to major cerebral artery occlusion. While very effective, it carries some risks, including cerebral air embolism, which can occur during the procedure. This rare complication, with an estimated incidence of 0.08%, is diagnosed primarily through clinical assessment and neuroimaging.
Methods: We present the case of a 68-year-old woman with hypertension who presented with sudden leftsided hemiparesis and facial drooping. Found unresponsive, she underwent a neurological examination revealing an NIHSS score of 15, with CT confirming right MCA occlusion, leading to mechanical thrombectomy. Post-thrombectomy, she developed delirium, and further investigation confirmed pneumocephalus on repeat CT. By day four, her condition improved, and she was transferred from ITU to her local hospital.
Results: Air can enter the arterial circulation due to MT procedural techniques. While pneumocephalus is rare after thrombectomy, it may arise from technical mishaps. Awareness and monitoring are required to identify these rare complications. In this case, the patient’s clinical decline was attributed to the combined effects of air embolism and mild subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Conclusions: Pneumocephalus is a rare but a possible complication of mechanical thrombectomy, typically with a good prognosis. This case highlights the importance of awareness of this complication, thorough post-procedural monitoring, and prompt diagnostic imaging to identify unforeseen issues, such as cerebral air embolism. Symptoms may not be immediately apparent, as the patient may have undergone the procedure under GA. It is also crucial to review local MT practices if such complications are frequent.

1Universidad Autonoma de Baja California, Tijuana, Mexico, 2Universidad Nacional de Piura, Piura, Peru, 3University of Minnesota, Departament Of Neurosurgery., twin cities, United States of America, 4Universidad Catolica Boliviana "San Pablo", Medicine, Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia, 5University Of Santander, Norte De Santander, CUCUTA, Colombia, 6Universidad Mexico Americana del Norte, Reynosa, Mexico, 7Universidad Católica Boliviana San Pablo, Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, Bolivia, 8Universidad Santiago de Cali, Valle Del Cauca, Cali, Colombia, 9Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, FES ZARAGOZA, Ciudad de México, Mexico, 10Instituto Nacional de Neurología y Neurocirugía, Ciudad de México, Mexico
Background and Aims: Evidence on the most effective treatment for stroke due to distal and medium vessel occlusions (DMVOs) remains unclear, as existing meta-analyses compare heterogeneous groups. We conducted a network meta-analysis to directly and indirectly compare different treatments for DMVOs.
Methods: We performed a comprehensive search of databases through April 2025 to identify studies comparing endovascular treatment (EVT) with other therapies in DMVOs. We included 31 studies with EVT, intravenous thrombolysis (IVT), medical management (MM), and conservative management (CM) groups. Outcomes assessed included 90-day favorable modified Rankin Scale (mRS0–2), symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH), and 90-day mortality.
Results: Compared to EVT, CM was associated with a lower rate of mRS 0–2 (RR:2.79, CI:95% 1.28–6.11, p= 0.01), while MM and IVT showed no significant differences. For mRS 3–6, CM (RR:3.05, CI:95% 1.43–6.55, p= 0.004) and IVT (RR:1.34, CI:95% 1.01–1.77, p= 0.04) carried greater risk than EVT. MM (RR: 0.59, CI:95% .35–1.00, p= 0.0498), IVT (RR:0.57, CI:95% 0.29–1.10, p= 0.10), and CM (RR:0.14, CI:95% 0.005–4.16, p = 0.26) showed non-significant lower sICH risk compared to EVT. No significant differences were found in 90-day mortality.
Conclusions: EVT consistently showed a favorable profile for mRS 0–2 at 90 days, with a non-significant increase in sICH, in 90-day mortality EVT group had lower risk than others therapies but non-statistically significant differences. These findings support EVT to improve functional recovery.

THROMBECTOMY.A. Aragon-Cortes1, D. Natera-Rodriguez2, L.E. Cueva Cañola3, R. Orozco4, Y. Flores Bravo5, M.D.L.L. Nevarez Rivera6, D. Pichardo Rojas4, D. López-Mena7

Background and Aims: Endovascular treatment (EVT) is the modality of treatment in select patients with acute ischemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion secondary to atherosclerosis (LVO-A). The evidence of adjunctive use of Tirofiban in LVO-A is relatively limited. We performed a meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of tirofiban in patients with LVO-A.
Methods: A database search was conducted until July 2024, to identify published studies that compare the use of Tirofiban in LVO-A to a control group. From a total of 1,541 studies, 1 randomized controlled trials, 9 cohorts and we also included 2 post-hoc analysis which reported additional outcomes to the original studies, without counting these duplicated patients into our final patient sample, encompassing a population of 3,393 patients. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that intraoperative tirofiban has the potential to reduce mortality, risk of reocclusion at 90-day and favorable 90-day mRS in patients with LVO-A. Large multicentric clinical trials are necessary to determined what is the dosis of Tirofiban, the ideal via and the moment of administration.

THROMBECTOMY.H. Atwan1, M.M. Alaref2, M.A. Bedewi3, O.A.M.A. Zidan2, A.S. Abdelwahed4, R.M. Odat5, R.M. Korish6, I. Khalil6, Y.M. Al Msalmeh7, D. Mounir8, K.A. Mohamed2, R. Abdelnaby9
1Faculty of Medicine, Assiut university, Assiut, Egypt, 2Faculty of Medicine, Cairo University, Cairo, Egypt, Cairo, Egypt, 3College of Medicine, Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University, Al-Kharj, Saudi Arabia, 4Nasser Institute Hospital for Research and Treatment, Cairo, Egypt, Cairo, Egypt, 5Faculty of Medicine, Jordan University of Science and Technology, Irbid, Jordan., Irbid, Jordan, 6Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University, Alexandria, Egypt, 7Mediclinic Alain Hospital, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, 8Faculty of Medicine, Suez Canal University, Suez, Egypt, 9University Hospital RWTH Aachen, Aachen, Germany
Background and Aims: Endovascular therapy, including Mechanical Thrombectomy (MT), has shown promising outcomes in the management of tandem lesions (TL). However, the benefit of adjunctive Intravenous Thrombolysis (IVT) remains controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis compares MT alone versus MT with IVT in patients with TL, providing a comprehensive evaluation of the associated advantages and risks.
Methods: A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase. Studies meeting predefined eligibility criteria were included. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed, followed by statistical analyses using RevMan 5.4 and Open Meta-Analyst to compare clinical outcomes between the MT-alone and MT+IVT groups. Sensitivity analyses were also conducted to ensure the robustness of the findings.
Results: Fourteen moderate-to-high-quality studies comprising 1,966 patients were included (1,064 received IVT+MT; 902 underwent MT alone). The IVT+MT group showed a significantly higher likelihood of achieving good functional outcomes (mRS 0–2; OR = 1.51) and successful reperfusion (TICI 2B–3; OR = 2.45). In contrast, the MT-alone group demonstrated higher 90-day mortality (OR = 0.55) and a greater risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH; OR = 0.72). Subgroup analyses suggested potential benefits of IVT+MT in specific patient populations, to be elaborated in the Results and Discussion sections.

Conclusions: Combining IVT with MT in patients with TL is associated with improved functional outcomes and increased reperfusion success. MT alone is linked to higher 90-day mortality and an elevated risk of sICH. Further high-quality studies are warranted to define optimal treatment strategies, particularly considering clot burden, anatomical variations, and pre-existing vascular conditions.

Background and Aims: The ATTENTION and BAOCHE trials demonstrated the efficacy of endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute basilar artery occlusion (BAO) in carefully selected populations.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of a nationwide, multicenter, prospectively collected stroke database. This study included patients with BAO who presented within 24 hours of the time last seen well (TLSW). Trial eligibility was assessed using the eligibility criteria of each trial including neuroimaging parameters. To evaluate the effectiveness of EVT, patients were categorized into three groups: ATTENTION-eligible, BAOCHE-eligible, and ineligible for both trials. DETERMINING THE OPTIMAL LOCATION FOR NEW EVT CENTRES IN CANADA TO MAXIMIZE TIMELY ACCESS TO EVT WHILE MAINTAINING SUFFICIENT CASES PER CENTRE
THROMBECTOMY.B. Baradaran-Noveiri
Dalhousie University, Industrial Engineering, Halifax, Canada
Background and Aims: Access to timely endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) is critical for reducing disability and death in patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) acute ischemic stroke. In Canada, geographic dispersion and infrastructure distribution pose challenges to EVT access, particularly in rural and remote areas. This study aims to determine the optimal location for new EVT centres in Canada while maintaining a sufficient number of EVT cases per centre.
Methods: Canada has 178 primary stroke centres (PSCs) and 27 comprehensive stroke centres (CSCs). These centres are mapped, and the country is divided into small geographic grid sections. Population data for each grid is obtained from ArcGIS. Using OpenStreetMap, drive times are calculated from each grid centroid to the nearest PSC and CSC, as well as between each PSC and its closest CSC. Grid sections where travel time to a CSC exceeds six hours are identified. DESTINE Health is used to generate these computations and corresponding maps. High-population, low-access areas are prioritized. A new CSC is assigned to the nearest PSC in each of these areas, and the model is rerun to evaluate the resulting improvements in population access.
Results: Initial analysis identifies multiple high-population areas with limited EVT access. Upgrading some PSCs to CSCs improves six-hour coverage within multiple provinces. Most new CSCs also maintain sufficient EVT case volumes.
Conclusions: This study uses geographic and population modeling to support stroke system planning by identifying CSC locations that improve EVT access while ensuring sustainability through adequate case volume.
